Deep Learning

Neural networks from a single neuron to CNNs, LSTMs, autoencoders and GANs — built from scratch in NumPy, then trained for real in PyTorch and Keras.

📚 21 Lessons  |  🔥 PyTorch · Keras · NumPy  |  ▶️ Every network on this page was trained by the code shown (on a CPU)  |  AI/ML Track
What you will learn in this module: how neural networks compute (neurons, activations, forward pass, losses), how they learn (backpropagation, gradient descent, optimizers), and how to train them well (initialisation, regularisation, batch norm, tuning, GPUs). Then the main architectures — CNNs for images, RNNs/LSTMs/GRUs for sequences, autoencoders and GANs for representation and generation — and the applied tasks of image classification, transfer learning, object detection and face recognition, ending with deployment, a project and interview questions. To keep this page self-contained, all examples use small built-in or generated datasets that train in seconds on a laptop CPU; the same code scales to real datasets on GPUs.
8.1

Neural Networks & the Perceptron

A neural network is a stack of simple units — artificial neurons — each computing a weighted sum of its inputs and passing it through a non-linear function. One neuron can only draw a straight line; layers of them can approximate almost any function. That's why the same idea works for photos, speech, text and tables, given enough data.

One Neuron

\[ z = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \dots + w_nx_n + b = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b \qquad\quad a = f(z) \]w = weights (importance of each input) · b = bias (shifts the threshold) · f = activation function · a = the neuron's output
Inputs x₁ … xₙ
→
× weights, + bias
→
activation f(z)
→
output a

The Perceptron (1958)

The original artificial neuron uses a step function: output 1 if \(z > 0\), else 0. Its learning rule nudges the weights whenever it makes a mistake: \(w \leftarrow w + \eta\,(y - \hat{y})\,x\).

Cell — a perceptron learns AND and OR, and fails at XORPython
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]])

def train_perceptron(X, y, epochs=20, lr=0.1):
    w, b = np.zeros(2), 0.0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
            pred = int(w @ xi + b > 0)
            w += lr * (yi - pred) * xi                 # update only when wrong
            b += lr * (yi - pred)
    return w, b, [int(w @ xi + b > 0) for xi in X]

for name, y in [("AND", [0, 0, 0, 1]), ("OR", [0, 1, 1, 1]), ("XOR", [0, 1, 1, 0])]:
    w, b, preds = train_perceptron(X, np.array(y))
    print(f"{name:<4} target {y}  learned {preds}  {'✓' if preds == y else '✗ not linearly separable'}   w={w.round(2)}, b={b:.1f}")
AND target [0, 0, 0, 1] learned [0, 0, 0, 1] ✓ w=[0.2 0.1], b=-0.2 OR target [0, 1, 1, 1] learned [0, 1, 1, 1] ✓ w=[0.1 0.1], b=0.0 XOR target [0, 1, 1, 0] learned [1, 1, 0, 0] ✗ not linearly separable w=[-0.1 0. ], b=0.1

XOR can't be separated by one straight line, so no single perceptron can learn it. That limitation (highlighted in 1969) stalled neural-network research for years — until networks with hidden layers and a way to train them (backpropagation, 8.4) arrived.

Layers: Input, Hidden, Output

In
Input layer
One value per feature (e.g. 64 pixel intensities); no computation
H
Hidden layers
Each neuron combines all outputs of the previous layer; layers learn increasingly abstract features (edges → shapes → objects)
Out
Output layer
1 neuron for regression or yes/no; one per class (with softmax) for multi-class
Cell — one hidden layer solves XOR (a small network trained with scikit-learn)Python
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
y_xor = [0, 1, 1, 0]
mlp = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(4,), activation="tanh", solver="lbfgs", random_state=1, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y_xor)
print("XOR with 4 hidden neurons:", mlp.predict(X).tolist())
n_params = sum(w.size for w in mlp.coefs_) + sum(b.size for b in mlp.intercepts_)
print("parameters:", n_params, "=", "2×4 weights + 4 biases + 4×1 weights + 1 bias")
XOR with 4 hidden neurons: [0, 1, 1, 0] parameters: 17 = 2×4 weights + 4 biases + 4×1 weights + 1 bias

Why "Deep" Learning Took Off

IngredientWhat changed (roughly 2006–2015)
DataInternet-scale labelled datasets (ImageNet: 14 million images)
ComputeGPUs made the matrix multiplications 10–100× faster
AlgorithmsReLU activations, better initialisation, dropout, batch norm, Adam, residual connections
SoftwareAutomatic differentiation frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch)

Classical ML (Module 7)

You engineer features; works best on tables; less data; faster; easier to explain. Gradient boosting often beats neural nets on tabular data.

Deep learning

Learns features from raw data; dominates images, audio, text, video; needs more data and compute; harder to interpret.

An artificial neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias and applies an activation function. The perceptron uses a step activation and a mistake-driven update rule; it learns linearly separable functions like AND and OR but cannot learn XOR, which requires hidden layers. A neural network stacks input, hidden and output layers so that later layers learn increasingly abstract features. Deep learning took off with large datasets, GPUs, better techniques (ReLU, initialisation, dropout, batch norm, Adam, residual connections) and autodiff frameworks; it dominates unstructured data, while gradient boosting often remains better on tables.
8.2

Activation Functions

Without activation functions, stacking layers is pointless: a linear layer of a linear layer is still one linear layer. The activation function adds the non-linearity that lets networks bend decision boundaries and model complex patterns. The choice also affects how well gradients flow during training.
Cell — the common activations and their slopesPython
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
z = np.linspace(-5, 5, 400)
sigmoid = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
acts = {
    "sigmoid": (sigmoid, sigmoid * (1 - sigmoid)),
    "tanh": (np.tanh(z), 1 - np.tanh(z) ** 2),
    "ReLU": (np.maximum(0, z), (z > 0).astype(float)),
    "Leaky ReLU": (np.where(z > 0, z, 0.05 * z), np.where(z > 0, 1, 0.05)),
    "GELU": (0.5 * z * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (z + 0.044715 * z ** 3))), None),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(13, 2.6), sharex=True)
for ax, (name, (f, d)) in zip(axes, acts.items()):
    ax.plot(z, f, color="#4ea8de", lw=2, label="f(z)")
    ax.plot(z, d if d is not None else np.gradient(f, z), color="#ffb454", ls="--", label="slope")
    ax.axhline(0, color="#3a4a5a", lw=0.8); ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
print("max slope of sigmoid:", (sigmoid * (1 - sigmoid)).max())
max slope of sigmoid: 0.2499901856200238
ActivationFormulaRangeWhere it's usedWatch out
ReLU\(\max(0, z)\)[0, ∞)Default for hidden layers (CNNs, MLPs)"Dead" neurons stuck at 0
Leaky ReLU / ELUsmall slope for z < 0(−∞, ∞)When many ReLUs dieOne extra hyperparameter
GELU / SiLU (Swish)smooth ReLU-like≈ (−0.2, ∞)Transformers, modern CNNsSlightly more compute
Sigmoid\(1/(1+e^{-z})\)(0, 1)Output for binary / multi-label; gates in LSTMsSaturates → vanishing gradients in deep stacks
Tanh\(\tanh z\)(−1, 1)RNN hidden statesAlso saturates
Softmax\(e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}\)probabilities summing to 1Output for multi-classUse with cross-entropy loss

Vanishing Gradients, in One Line of Arithmetic

Cell — the gradient reaching the first layer is a product of slopesPython
for layers in (5, 10, 20):
    print(f"{layers:>2} layers: sigmoid best case {0.25 ** layers:.2e}   ReLU (active units) {1.0 ** layers:.0f}")
5 layers: sigmoid best case 9.77e-04 ReLU (active units) 1 10 layers: sigmoid best case 9.54e-07 ReLU (active units) 1 20 layers: sigmoid best case 9.09e-13 ReLU (active units) 1

Sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so through 20 layers the learning signal shrinks by a factor of 10¹². ReLU's slope is exactly 1 for active units, which is a big reason it made deep networks trainable.

Softmax for Multi-Class Output

CellPython
def softmax(z):
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())                       # subtract the max for numerical stability
    return e / e.sum()
logits = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])               # raw scores for cat, dog, bird
print("probabilities:", softmax(logits).round(3), "sum =", softmax(logits).sum())
print("with large logits (no overflow):", softmax(np.array([1000.0, 999.0, 998.0])).round(3))
probabilities: [0.659 0.242 0.099] sum = 1.0 with large logits (no overflow): [0.665 0.245 0.09 ]
Activation functions add non-linearity; without them any stack of layers collapses into one linear transformation. ReLU is the default for hidden layers because it is cheap and passes gradients unchanged for positive inputs, though units can die (Leaky ReLU or ELU help); GELU and SiLU are smooth variants used in transformers. Sigmoid and tanh saturate, so their small derivatives (sigmoid at most 0.25) multiply into vanishing gradients in deep networks, but sigmoid remains the output for binary or multi-label tasks and inside LSTM gates. Softmax converts logits into class probabilities for multi-class outputs, and regression outputs use no activation.
8.3

Forward Propagation & Loss Functions

Forward propagation is how a network makes a prediction: data flows layer by layer, each one a matrix multiplication, a bias and an activation. A loss function then scores how wrong the prediction is. Training (next lessons) is nothing more than adjusting weights to make that loss smaller.

A Layer Is a Matrix Multiplication

\[ \mathbf{a}^{[0]} = \mathbf{x}, \qquad \mathbf{z}^{[l]} = \mathbf{a}^{[l-1]} W^{[l]} + \mathbf{b}^{[l]}, \qquad \mathbf{a}^{[l]} = f^{[l]}(\mathbf{z}^{[l]}) \]for a batch of m examples, \(a^{[l-1]}\) is (m × n_in), W is (n_in × n_out), b is (n_out) — one matrix product handles the whole batch
Cell — forward pass of a 4 → 5 → 3 network on a batch, by handPython
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
X = rng.normal(size=(2, 4))                           # batch of 2 examples, 4 features
W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (4, 5)), np.zeros(5)     # layer 1: 4 → 5
W2, b2 = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (5, 3)), np.zeros(3)     # layer 2: 5 → 3 classes

z1 = X @ W1 + b1;  a1 = np.maximum(0, z1)            # hidden layer, ReLU
z2 = a1 @ W2 + b2                                     # output logits
probs = np.exp(z2 - z2.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)); probs /= probs.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
for name, arr in [("X", X), ("z1", z1), ("a1", a1), ("logits z2", z2), ("softmax", probs)]:
    print(f"{name:<10} shape {arr.shape}  first row {arr[0].round(2)}")
print("parameters:", W1.size + b1.size + W2.size + b2.size)
X shape (2, 4) first row [ 2.04 -2.56 0.42 -0.57] z1 shape (2, 5) first row [ 0.31 4.75 0.58 -1.2 0.21] a1 shape (2, 5) first row [0.31 4.75 0.58 0. 0.21] logits z2 shape (2, 3) first row [-0.68 2.52 0.37] softmax shape (2, 3) first row [0.04 0.86 0.1 ] parameters: 43

Loss Functions

TaskOutput layerLossFormula
RegressionLinearMean squared error (or MAE / Huber for outliers)\(\frac{1}{m}\sum (y - \hat{y})^2\)
Binary classification1 unit + sigmoidBinary cross-entropy\(-[y\log\hat{p} + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{p})]\)
Multi-classK units + softmaxCategorical cross-entropy\(-\log \hat{p}_{\text{true class}}\)
Multi-labelK units + sigmoid eachBinary cross-entropy per labelsum over labels
Cell — cross-entropy punishes confident mistakes hardPython
true_class = 0
for p in (0.95, 0.7, 0.4, 0.1, 0.01):
    print(f"P(true class) = {p:<5} → loss {-np.log(p):.3f}")
y = np.array([0, 2]); print("\nbatch loss for our 2 examples:", round(float(-np.log(probs[np.arange(2), y]).mean()), 3),
                            f"(random guessing among 3 classes = {np.log(3):.3f})")
P(true class) = 0.95 → loss 0.051 P(true class) = 0.7 → loss 0.357 P(true class) = 0.4 → loss 0.916 P(true class) = 0.1 → loss 2.303 P(true class) = 0.01 → loss 4.605 batch loss for our 2 examples: 2.221 (random guessing among 3 classes = 1.099)
In PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits and applies softmax internally (more numerically stable) — don't add your own softmax layer before it. Likewise use BCEWithLogitsLoss rather than sigmoid + BCELoss.
Forward propagation computes each layer as a matrix product of the previous activations with a weight matrix plus a bias, followed by an activation function, processing whole batches at once; output logits become probabilities through softmax or sigmoid. The loss measures error: mean squared error (or MAE/Huber) for regression, binary cross-entropy with a sigmoid output for binary or multi-label tasks, and categorical cross-entropy with softmax for multi-class, where the loss is the negative log probability of the true class and grows sharply for confident mistakes. Frameworks combine softmax or sigmoid with the loss for numerical stability, so models output raw logits.
8.4

Backpropagation

To improve, every weight needs to know: if I change a little, how does the loss change? Backpropagation answers that for millions of weights in one backward sweep, by applying the calculus chain rule (Module 3.10) from the loss back to the first layer and reusing intermediate results. Frameworks do it automatically, but building it once by hand removes the mystery.

The Chain Rule Through a Network

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[1]}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial a^{[2]}} \cdot \frac{\partial a^{[2]}}{\partial z^{[2]}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{[2]}}{\partial a^{[1]}} \cdot \frac{\partial a^{[1]}}{\partial z^{[1]}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{[1]}}{\partial W^{[1]}} \]with softmax + cross-entropy, the first two factors simplify beautifully to \(\hat{p} - y\)
Forward: x → z¹ → a¹ → z² → p̂ → loss
→
Backward: ∂L/∂z² = p̂ − y → ∂L/∂W² → ∂L/∂a¹ → ∂L/∂z¹ → ∂L/∂W¹
→
Update: W ← W − η·∂L/∂W

A Network From Scratch in NumPy

Cell — 2-layer network learns a curved boundaryPython
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
X, y = make_moons(n_samples=400, noise=0.15, random_state=0)
Y = np.eye(2)[y]                                             # one-hot targets
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
W1 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / 2), (2, 16)); b1 = np.zeros(16)
W2 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / 16), (16, 2)); b2 = np.zeros(2)
lr, m = 0.5, len(X)

for epoch in range(2001):
    # forward
    z1 = X @ W1 + b1; a1 = np.maximum(0, z1)
    z2 = a1 @ W2 + b2
    p = np.exp(z2 - z2.max(1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    loss = -np.log(p[np.arange(m), y]).mean()
    # backward (chain rule, layer by layer)
    dz2 = (p - Y) / m                                        # softmax + cross-entropy gradient
    dW2, db2 = a1.T @ dz2, dz2.sum(0)
    da1 = dz2 @ W2.T
    dz1 = da1 * (z1 > 0)                                     # ReLU passes gradient only where active
    dW1, db1 = X.T @ dz1, dz1.sum(0)
    # update
    W1 -= lr * dW1; b1 -= lr * db1; W2 -= lr * dW2; b2 -= lr * db2
    if epoch in (0, 100, 500, 2000):
        print(f"epoch {epoch:>4}  loss {loss:.4f}  accuracy {(p.argmax(1) == y).mean():.3f}")

xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.5, 2.5, 200), np.linspace(-1, 1.5, 200))
grid = np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()]
Z = (np.maximum(0, grid @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2).argmax(1).reshape(xx.shape)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.contourf(xx, yy, Z, alpha=0.3, cmap="coolwarm"); ax.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=y, s=6, cmap="coolwarm")
ax.set_title("decision boundary learned by hand-written backprop", fontsize=9); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
epoch 0 loss 0.7284 accuracy 0.625 epoch 100 loss 0.1695 accuracy 0.940 epoch 500 loss 0.0452 accuracy 0.988 epoch 2000 loss 0.0308 accuracy 0.985

Checking Gradients — and Letting Autograd Do It

Cell — numerical check, then PyTorch autograd gives the same gradientPython
def loss_fn(W1_):
    a = np.maximum(0, X @ W1_ + b1); z = a @ W2 + b2
    q = np.exp(z - z.max(1, keepdims=True)); q /= q.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    return -np.log(q[np.arange(m), y]).mean()

z1 = X @ W1 + b1; a1 = np.maximum(0, z1); z2 = a1 @ W2 + b2
p = np.exp(z2 - z2.max(1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
analytic = (X.T @ (((p - Y) / m) @ W2.T * (z1 > 0)))[0, 0]
eps = 1e-5; Wp, Wm = W1.copy(), W1.copy(); Wp[0, 0] += eps; Wm[0, 0] -= eps
numeric = (loss_fn(Wp) - loss_fn(Wm)) / (2 * eps)

import torch
tW1 = torch.tensor(W1, requires_grad=True)
tz = torch.relu(torch.tensor(X) @ tW1 + torch.tensor(b1)) @ torch.tensor(W2) + torch.tensor(b2)
torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(tz, torch.tensor(y)).backward()          # autograd: one line
print(f"∂L/∂W1[0,0]  backprop {analytic:.8f}   numerical {numeric:.8f}   PyTorch autograd {tW1.grad[0, 0].item():.8f}")
∂L/∂W1[0,0] backprop -0.00000883 numerical -0.00000883 PyTorch autograd -0.00000883

All three agree. In practice you never write the backward pass: frameworks record the forward operations as a computational graph and differentiate it automatically (autograd). Knowing what it does helps you debug exploding/vanishing gradients and understand why some architectures train better.

Gradient Problems

ProblemCauseFixes
Vanishing gradientsMany small factors multiplied (sigmoid/tanh, long RNNs)ReLU-family activations, good initialisation, batch/layer norm, residual connections, LSTM/GRU
Exploding gradientsMany large factors (deep or recurrent nets)Gradient clipping, smaller learning rate, normalisation
Dead ReLUsUnits pushed permanently negativeLower learning rate, Leaky ReLU, careful init
Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backwards from the loss through each layer, reusing intermediate values from the forward pass; with softmax and cross-entropy the output gradient is simply predicted probabilities minus one-hot targets, and ReLU passes gradients only where units were active. Gradients are then used by gradient descent to update weights. Frameworks implement this automatically with autograd over a computational graph, and hand-written gradients can be verified numerically. Vanishing and exploding gradients are mitigated with ReLU, careful initialisation, normalisation, residual connections, gated RNNs and gradient clipping.
8.5

Gradient Descent & Optimizers

Backpropagation gives the direction of steepest increase of the loss; gradient descent steps the opposite way. How big each step is (the learning rate), how many examples you use per step (batch size), and how you smooth and scale the steps (the optimizer) decide whether training is fast, slow or diverges.
\[ w \leftarrow w - \eta\, \nabla_w L \qquad\quad \text{Adam: } m \leftarrow \beta_1 m + (1-\beta_1) g, \;\; v \leftarrow \beta_2 v + (1-\beta_2) g^2, \;\; w \leftarrow w - \eta \frac{\hat{m}}{\sqrt{\hat{v}} + \epsilon} \]η = learning rate · g = gradient · Adam keeps a running mean (momentum) and running mean square (per-weight scale) of gradients

Batch, Mini-Batch and Stochastic

VariantExamples per updateBehaviour
Batch gradient descentAll of themSmooth but slow; impossible for big data
Stochastic (SGD)1Very noisy; noise can help escape bad regions
Mini-batch (the standard)32–1024Efficient on GPUs; balanced noise. One pass over the data = one epoch

The Learning Rate Matters Most

Cell — minimising a narrow valley f(x, y) = x² + 10y²Python
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
grad = lambda p: np.array([2 * p[0], 20 * p[1]])
f = lambda p: p[0] ** 2 + 10 * p[1] ** 2

def run(opt, lr, steps=60):
    p, path, m, v = np.array([-4.0, 1.5]), [], np.zeros(2), np.zeros(2)
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        path.append(p.copy()); g = grad(p)
        if opt == "sgd":
            p = p - lr * g
        elif opt == "momentum":
            m = 0.9 * m + g; p = p - lr * m
        elif opt == "adam":
            m = 0.9 * m + 0.1 * g; v = 0.999 * v + 0.001 * g ** 2
            p = p - lr * (m / (1 - 0.9 ** t)) / (np.sqrt(v / (1 - 0.999 ** t)) + 1e-8)
    return np.array(path), f(p)

xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-5, 5, 200), np.linspace(-2, 2, 200))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 2.8))
for ax, (title, opt, lr) in zip(axes, [("SGD lr=0.02 (too small)", "sgd", 0.02), ("SGD lr=0.095 (zig-zag)", "sgd", 0.095),
                                       ("Momentum lr=0.02", "momentum", 0.02), ("Adam lr=0.3", "adam", 0.3)]):
    path, final = run(opt, lr)
    ax.contour(xx, yy, xx ** 2 + 10 * yy ** 2, levels=15, colors="#3a4a5a", linewidths=0.6)
    ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], marker=".", color="#ffb454", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nloss after 60 steps {final:.3g}", fontsize=8); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
print("lr=0.11 →", f"{run('sgd', 0.11)[1]:.3g}", "(diverges: the steep direction overshoots more each step)")
lr=0.11 → 7.14e+10 (diverges: the steep direction overshoots more each step)

Optimizers

OptimizerIdeaTypical use
SGDPlain step down the gradientBaseline
SGD + momentum (Nesterov)Accumulate velocity; dampens zig-zagsCNNs for images — often the best final accuracy with a good schedule
RMSpropDivide by running RMS of gradients (per-weight step size)RNNs historically
Adam / AdamWMomentum + RMS scaling + bias correction; AdamW decouples weight decayDefault for most work; transformers use AdamW

Learning-Rate Schedules

Cell — common schedules in PyTorchPython
import torch
def lrs(make_sched, epochs=50):
    opt = torch.optim.SGD([torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)], lr=0.1)
    s = make_sched(opt); out = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        out.append(opt.param_groups[0]["lr"]); opt.step(); s.step()
    return out
schedules = {"step decay (÷10 every 20)": lambda o: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(o, 20, 0.1),
             "cosine annealing": lambda o: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(o, 50),
             "one-cycle (warm-up then decay)": lambda o: torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(o, max_lr=0.1, total_steps=50)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.6))
for (name, mk), c in zip(schedules.items(), ["#4ea8de", "#ffb454", "#6de5a0"]):
    ax.plot(lrs(mk), label=name, color=c, lw=2)
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("learning rate"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
Practical defaults: AdamW with lr ≈ 1e-3 (1e-4–5e-5 for fine-tuning pretrained models), batch size 32–256, a warm-up plus cosine decay schedule, and early stopping on validation loss. If loss explodes, lower the learning rate first.
Gradient descent updates weights opposite the gradient scaled by the learning rate; mini-batch gradient descent, using batches of tens to hundreds of examples per update and many epochs, is standard. Too small a learning rate is slow, too large oscillates or diverges, especially across directions of different curvature. Momentum accumulates velocity to damp zig-zags; RMSprop scales steps per weight; Adam combines both with bias correction and AdamW decouples weight decay, making it the common default. Learning-rate schedules such as step decay, cosine annealing and one-cycle warm-up improve convergence.
8.6

PyTorch, TensorFlow & Keras

Deep-learning frameworks give you three things: tensors (NumPy-like arrays that can live on a GPU), automatic differentiation, and building blocks (layers, losses, optimizers, data loaders). PyTorch dominates research and most new projects; TensorFlow is widespread in production and mobile; Keras is the high-level API that (since Keras 3) runs on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX. This lesson builds the same digit classifier in each style.

Tensors and Autograd

Cell — PyTorch basicsPython
import torch, numpy as np
torch.manual_seed(0); torch.set_num_threads(2)
t = torch.tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]])
print(t.shape, t.dtype, "| t @ t.T =", (t @ t.T).tolist())
print("from NumPy and back:", torch.from_numpy(np.arange(3.0)).numpy())
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
print("device available here:", device)

w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)          # track operations on w
loss = (2 * w - 4) ** 2
loss.backward()                                    # d/dw (2w − 4)² = 4(2w − 4) = 8 at w = 3
print("gradient:", w.grad.item())
torch.Size([2, 2]) torch.float32 | t @ t.T = [[5.0, 11.0], [11.0, 25.0]] from NumPy and back: [0. 1. 2.] device available here: cpu gradient: 8.0

The Data: 8×8 Handwritten Digits

Cell — prepare tensors and DataLoadersPython
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader
digits = load_digits()
X = digits.images.reshape(-1, 64).astype("float32") / 16.0          # scale pixels to 0–1
y = digits.target
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)
train_dl = DataLoader(TensorDataset(torch.tensor(X_tr), torch.tensor(y_tr)), batch_size=64, shuffle=True)
test_X, test_y = torch.tensor(X_te), torch.tensor(y_te)
print(f"{len(X_tr)} training images, {len(X_te)} test images, {len(train_dl)} mini-batches per epoch")
1347 training images, 450 test images, 22 mini-batches per epoch

PyTorch: Define, then Write the Training Loop

Cell — nn.Module + explicit loopPython
import torch.nn as nn
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)                                  # raw logits

model = MLP().to(device)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))

for epoch in range(1, 16):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in train_dl:
        xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
        opt.zero_grad()                     # 1. clear old gradients
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)       # 2. forward + loss
        loss.backward()                     # 3. backprop
        opt.step()                          # 4. update weights
    if epoch % 5 == 0:
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():               # no gradient tracking for evaluation
            acc = (model(test_X.to(device)).argmax(1).cpu() == test_y).float().mean().item()
        print(f"epoch {epoch:>2}  last batch loss {loss.item():.4f}  test accuracy {acc:.3f}")
parameters: 17226 epoch 5 last batch loss 0.4073 test accuracy 0.893 epoch 10 last batch loss 0.0898 test accuracy 0.931 epoch 15 last batch loss 0.0549 test accuracy 0.951

The four-line loop — zero grads, forward, backward, step — is the heart of every PyTorch program, from this toy to LLM training. model.train()/model.eval() switch layers like dropout and batch norm between training and inference behaviour.

Keras: Compile and Fit

Cell — the same network in Keras 3 (running here on the PyTorch backend)Python
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "torch"            # "tensorflow" or "jax" work identically
import keras, numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
d = load_digits()
X = d.images.reshape(-1, 64).astype("float32") / 16.0
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, d.target, test_size=0.25, stratify=d.target, random_state=0)

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(64,)),
                          keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
                          keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
                          keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
history = model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, epochs=15, batch_size=64, validation_split=0.1, verbose=0)
print(f"backend: {keras.backend.backend()}   parameters: {model.count_params()}")
print(f"final val accuracy {history.history['val_accuracy'][-1]:.3f}   test accuracy {model.evaluate(X_te, y_te, verbose=0)[1]:.3f}")
backend: torch parameters: 17226 final val accuracy 0.978 test accuracy 0.964

The TensorFlow Equivalent

import tensorflow as tf
model = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
                             tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
                             tf.keras.layers.Dense(10)])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=tf.keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, epochs=15, batch_size=64, validation_split=0.1)

# custom training step (the TensorFlow version of the PyTorch loop)
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    loss = loss_fn(yb, model(xb, training=True))
grads = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(grads, model.trainable_variables))

Which to Learn?

PyTorchTensorFlowKeras 3
StylePythonic, explicit loops, easy debuggingGraph compilation (tf.function), production toolingHighest-level: compile/fit; backend-agnostic
StrengthsResearch, LLMs, Hugging Face ecosystem, most new papersTF Serving, TFLite (mobile/edge), TF.jsFastest to write; switch backends without code changes
Training loopYou write it (or use Lightning)fit or GradientTapefit

The concepts are identical across all three. This module uses PyTorch for most examples because it makes each step visible.

Deep-learning frameworks provide GPU-capable tensors, automatic differentiation and building blocks. In PyTorch, models subclass nn.Module, data flows through Dataset and DataLoader in mini-batches, and the training loop zeroes gradients, runs the forward pass and loss, calls backward and steps the optimizer, with model.train/eval and torch.no_grad for evaluation. Keras defines models with Sequential or functional APIs and trains with compile and fit, and Keras 3 runs on TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX backends; TensorFlow uses GradientTape for custom loops and offers production tooling such as TF Serving and TFLite. PyTorch dominates research and LLM work.
8.7

Training Deep Networks Well

Neural networks have far more parameters than training examples, so they overfit easily, and deep ones can be hard to train at all. A standard toolkit addresses both: good initialisation, normalisation layers, dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, early stopping and residual connections. This lesson shows each one's effect.

A Setup That Overfits

Cell — few training images, a big networkPython
import torch, torch.nn as nn, numpy as np, copy
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
torch.set_num_threads(2)
d = load_digits()
X = torch.tensor(d.images.reshape(-1, 64) / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32); y = torch.tensor(d.target)
idx_tr, idx_va = train_test_split(np.arange(len(y)), train_size=300, stratify=d.target, random_state=0)   # only 300 to train

def make(dropout=0.0, batchnorm=False):
    layers, width = [], 64
    for h in (512, 512):
        layers += [nn.Linear(width, h)] + ([nn.BatchNorm1d(h)] if batchnorm else []) + [nn.ReLU()]
        layers += [nn.Dropout(dropout)] if dropout else []
        width = h
    return nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(width, 10))

def train(model, epochs=150, wd=0.0, patience=None, lr=1e-3):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=wd)
    hist, best, best_state, wait = [], 9e9, None, 0
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model.train(); perm = torch.randperm(300)
        for i in range(0, 300, 32):
            b = idx_tr[perm[i:i + 32].numpy()]
            opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[b]), y[b]).backward(); opt.step()
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            tr = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[idx_tr]), y[idx_tr]).item()
            va = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[idx_va]), y[idx_va]).item()
            acc = (model(X[idx_va]).argmax(1) == y[idx_va]).float().mean().item()
        hist.append((tr, va, acc))
        if patience is not None:
            if va < best: best, best_state, wait = va, copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()), 0
            else:
                wait += 1
                if wait >= patience: model.load_state_dict(best_state); break
    return np.array(hist)

torch.manual_seed(0); plain = train(make())
print(f"plain: final train loss {plain[-1, 0]:.4f}, validation loss min {plain[:, 1].min():.3f} → final {plain[-1, 1]:.3f}, val acc {plain[-1, 2]:.3f}")
plain: final train loss 0.0002, validation loss min 0.214 → final 0.303, val acc 0.941

The Toolkit, Measured

Cell — compare regularisers on the same dataPython
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
runs = {"plain": plain}
torch.manual_seed(0); runs["dropout 0.5"] = train(make(dropout=0.5))
torch.manual_seed(0); runs["weight decay 0.05"] = train(make(), wd=0.05)
torch.manual_seed(0); runs["batch norm"] = train(make(batchnorm=True))
torch.manual_seed(0); runs["early stopping (patience 10)"] = train(make(), patience=10)
for name, h in runs.items():
    print(f"{name:<30} epochs {len(h):>3}  final val loss {h[-1, 1]:.3f}  val acc {h[-1, 2]:.3f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
for (name, h), c in zip(runs.items(), ["#ff7c7c", "#4ea8de", "#6de5a0", "#ffb454", "#c39bd3"]):
    ax.plot(h[:, 1], label=name, color=c)
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("validation loss"); ax.set_ylim(0, 0.8); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plain epochs 150 final val loss 0.303 val acc 0.941 dropout 0.5 epochs 150 final val loss 0.266 val acc 0.944 weight decay 0.05 epochs 150 final val loss 0.283 val acc 0.943 batch norm epochs 150 final val loss 0.199 val acc 0.949 early stopping (patience 10) epochs 27 final val loss 0.227 val acc 0.947

The plain network's validation loss bottoms out early and then climbs as it memorises 300 images. Each technique holds that rise back. (With early stopping the restored model is the one from the best epoch.) In practice they're combined.

TechniqueWhat it doesTypical setting
Initialisation (He / Xavier)Scales starting weights so signals neither explode nor vanishHe (Kaiming) for ReLU — framework default
Batch normalisationNormalises each layer's inputs per mini-batch; faster, more stable trainingCNNs, MLPs (LayerNorm in transformers and RNNs)
DropoutRandomly zeroes units during training so the network can't rely on any one0.1–0.5; off at inference
Weight decay (L2)Penalises large weights1e-4 – 1e-2 with AdamW
Data augmentationCreates varied copies of training data (flips, crops, noise)Images, audio (8.11)
Early stoppingStop when validation loss stops improving; keep the best weightsPatience 5–20 epochs
Residual connectionsout = x + layer(x): gradients flow straight through; enables 100+ layersResNets, transformers
Gradient clippingCaps gradient normRNNs, transformers (max norm 1.0)

Debugging Training

  • First, overfit one small batch — if the loss won't go near zero, there's a bug (wrong labels, loss, or shapes)
  • Loss is NaN or explodes → lower the learning rate, check inputs for NaN/inf, clip gradients
  • Loss stuck at log(#classes) → the network predicts uniformly: check learning rate, data shuffling, label alignment
  • Training loss falls, validation rises → overfitting: regularise, augment, get more data
  • Both high → underfitting: bigger model, train longer, higher learning rate
Deep networks overfit and can be hard to optimise, so training uses He or Xavier initialisation to keep activations stable, batch normalisation (or layer normalisation) to stabilise and speed training, dropout to prevent co-adaptation of units (disabled at inference), weight decay to penalise large weights, data augmentation to enlarge the training set, early stopping that restores the best validation checkpoint, residual connections so gradients flow through very deep networks, and gradient clipping against explosions. Debugging starts by overfitting a single batch and reading training versus validation loss curves.
8.8

Hyperparameter Tuning for Deep Learning

Neural networks have many knobs — learning rate, batch size, width, depth, dropout, weight decay, epochs — and each training run is expensive. The goal is to find a good configuration with as few runs as possible: tune the most important knobs first, search on a log scale, use small budgets to discard bad trials early, and let tools like Optuna do the bookkeeping.

What Matters Most

PriorityHyperparameterSearch range
1Learning rate1e-5 … 1e-1, log scale
2Batch size (with learning rate)16 … 512
2Model size: width, depthPowers of 2
3Regularisation: dropout, weight decay0–0.5; 1e-6 … 1e-1 log
3Optimizer settings, schedule, warm-upUsually defaults are fine

Learning-Rate Range Test

Cell — sweep the learning rate over one short runPython
import torch, torch.nn as nn, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
torch.set_num_threads(2); torch.manual_seed(0)
d = load_digits()
X = torch.tensor(d.images.reshape(-1, 64) / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32); y = torch.tensor(d.target)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 10))
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=1e-5)
lrs = np.geomspace(1e-5, 10, 120); losses = []
for lr in lrs:
    for g in opt.param_groups: g["lr"] = lr
    b = torch.randint(0, len(y), (64,))
    loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(X[b]), y[b])
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); losses.append(loss.item())
smooth = np.convolve(losses, np.ones(5) / 5, mode="same")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
ax.plot(lrs, smooth, color="#4ea8de"); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(0, 4)
ax.set_xlabel("learning rate"); ax.set_ylabel("loss (smoothed)")
steepest = lrs[np.argmin(np.gradient(smooth[5:-5])) + 5]
ax.axvline(steepest, ls=":", color="#ffb454"); ax.set_title(f"loss falls fastest near lr ≈ {steepest:.2g}; pick a bit below where it blows up", fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()

Automated Search with Optuna

Cell — Bayesian search with early pruning of weak trialsPython
import optuna
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)
tr, va = train_test_split(np.arange(len(y)), test_size=0.25, stratify=d.target, random_state=0)

def objective(trial):
    lr = trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-4, 3e-2, log=True)
    width = trial.suggest_categorical("width", [32, 64, 128, 256])
    dropout = trial.suggest_float("dropout", 0.0, 0.5)
    wd = trial.suggest_float("weight_decay", 1e-6, 1e-2, log=True)
    torch.manual_seed(trial.number)
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, width), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(dropout), nn.Linear(width, 10))
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(net.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=wd)
    for epoch in range(20):
        net.train(); perm = tr[torch.randperm(len(tr)).numpy()]
        for i in range(0, len(perm), 64):
            b = perm[i:i + 64]; opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(X[b]), y[b]).backward(); opt.step()
        net.eval()
        with torch.no_grad(): acc = (net(X[va]).argmax(1) == y[va]).float().mean().item()
        trial.report(acc, epoch)
        if trial.should_prune(): raise optuna.TrialPruned()          # stop hopeless trials early
    return acc

study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize", sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0),
                            pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_warmup_steps=5))
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=25)
pruned = sum(t.state == optuna.trial.TrialState.PRUNED for t in study.trials)
print(f"best validation accuracy {study.best_value:.3f} with", {k: (round(v, 5) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in study.best_params.items()})
print(f"{pruned} of 25 trials stopped early by the pruner")
best validation accuracy 0.984 with {'lr': 0.0168, 'width': 256, 'dropout': 0.26747, 'weight_decay': 1e-05} 7 of 25 trials stopped early by the pruner
  • Random or Bayesian search beats grid search: most hyperparameters barely matter, so don't waste runs on them
  • Search on small data / few epochs first; confirm the best few at full scale
  • Fix seeds, but check the winner across 2–3 seeds — differences smaller than seed noise aren't real
  • Log every run (MLflow, Weights & Biases) so results are comparable and reproducible
Deep-learning tuning prioritises the learning rate, then batch size and model size, then regularisation (dropout, weight decay) and schedules. Searches use log-scaled ranges with random or Bayesian methods rather than grids, a learning-rate range test to find a sensible starting rate, and early pruning of weak trials (Optuna with TPE sampling and a median pruner, or Hyperband) to save compute. Candidates are screened cheaply on smaller data or fewer epochs, confirmed at full scale across several seeds, and all runs are logged for reproducibility.
8.9

GPU Training & Performance

Neural-network training is mostly huge matrix multiplications, and a GPU does thousands of multiply-adds in parallel. Moving the same code to a GPU often makes it 10–50× faster. This lesson covers putting work on the device, keeping the GPU fed with data, mixed precision, and the memory limits you'll hit. (This page was built on a CPU; the code below picks a GPU automatically if one is available.)

Why GPUs: Matrix Multiplication Scaling

Cell — throughput of matrix multiplication on this machinePython
import torch, time
torch.set_num_threads(2)
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu")
print("device:", device)
for n in (256, 1024, 2048):
    a, b = torch.randn(n, n, device=device), torch.randn(n, n, device=device)
    torch.mm(a, b)                                        # warm-up
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(5): c = torch.mm(a, b)
    if device.type == "cuda": torch.cuda.synchronize()    # GPU calls are asynchronous
    dt = (time.perf_counter() - t) / 5
    print(f"{n}×{n} matmul: {dt * 1000:7.1f} ms  ≈ {2 * n ** 3 / dt / 1e9:6.1f} GFLOP/s")
print("\nfor scale: a modern data-centre GPU sustains roughly 100,000+ GFLOP/s in reduced precision")
device: cpu 256×256 matmul: 0.1 ms ≈ 321.6 GFLOP/s 1024×1024 matmul: 6.7 ms ≈ 319.2 GFLOP/s 2048×2048 matmul: 51.4 ms ≈ 334.1 GFLOP/s for scale: a modern data-centre GPU sustains roughly 100,000+ GFLOP/s in reduced precision

The Device Pattern

device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model = MyModel().to(device)                              # move parameters once
for xb, yb in loader:
    xb, yb = xb.to(device, non_blocking=True), yb.to(device, non_blocking=True)   # move each batch
    ...
preds = model(xb).cpu().numpy()                            # bring results back for NumPy/pandas
"Expected all tensors to be on the same device" is the most common GPU error: the model and every tensor it touches must be on the same device.

Mixed Precision and Other Speed-Ups

Cell — automatic mixed precision (bfloat16 here on CPU; float16/bfloat16 on GPU)Python
import torch.nn as nn
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1024, 4096), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4096, 1024)).to(device)
x = torch.randn(512, 1024, device=device)
with torch.autocast(device_type=device.type, dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    out = model(x)
print("weights stored as", next(model.parameters()).dtype, "| matmuls computed in", out.dtype)
print(f"memory per parameter: float32 {torch.finfo(torch.float32).bits // 8} bytes, bfloat16 {torch.finfo(torch.bfloat16).bits // 8} bytes")
params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"this model: {params / 1e6:.1f}M parameters ≈ {params * 4 / 1e6:.0f} MB in float32; "
      f"training with Adam needs ≈ 4× that (weights, gradients, 2 optimizer states) + activations")
weights stored as torch.float32 | matmuls computed in torch.bfloat16 memory per parameter: float32 4 bytes, bfloat16 2 bytes this model: 8.4M parameters ≈ 34 MB in float32; training with Adam needs ≈ 4× that (weights, gradients, 2 optimizer states) + activations
TechniqueBenefit
Mixed precision (torch.autocast, bf16/fp16)~2× speed, half the activation memory, on modern GPUs
DataLoader num_workers, pin_memoryPrepare the next batches while the GPU computes — avoid a starved GPU
Bigger batches (with learning-rate scaling)Better GPU utilisation
Gradient accumulationSimulate a large batch when memory is short
torch.compile(model)Fuses operations into faster kernels
Gradient checkpointingTrade compute for memory on very deep models
Multi-GPU (DDP), FSDP / DeepSpeedData parallelism across GPUs; sharding for models too big for one GPU

Where to Get a GPU

  • Free tiers: Google Colab, Kaggle notebooks — enough for learning and small projects
  • Cloud: Azure ML, AWS SageMaker, Google Vertex AI, or plain GPU VMs (Module 10)
  • Check utilisation with nvidia-smi; if it's low, the data pipeline is the bottleneck
  • "CUDA out of memory" → smaller batch, mixed precision, gradient accumulation or checkpointing
GPUs accelerate deep learning because training is dominated by parallel matrix multiplications; in PyTorch the model and every batch are moved to the same device with .to(device), and results are returned to the CPU for NumPy. Throughput improves with mixed precision via autocast (bfloat16 or float16 with loss scaling), DataLoader workers and pinned memory to keep the GPU fed, larger batches, torch.compile, gradient accumulation and checkpointing for memory limits, and DDP or FSDP across multiple GPUs. Training memory is roughly weights, gradients and optimizer states (about four times the weights with Adam) plus activations.
8.10

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)

A dense network treats an image as a flat list of pixels and ignores which pixels are neighbours. A CNN slides small learnable filters across the image, so the same edge or texture detector is reused everywhere. Stacked, these layers learn edges, then shapes, then objects — with far fewer parameters. CNNs power image classification, medical imaging, quality inspection and the vision parts of self-driving systems.

Convolution: A Sliding Filter

\[ (I * K)(i, j) = \sum_{u}\sum_{v} I(i+u,\, j+v)\, K(u, v) \qquad\quad \text{output size} = \frac{n + 2p - k}{s} + 1 \]n = input size, k = filter size, p = padding, s = stride
Cell — hand-made edge filters on a digitPython
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt, torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
torch.set_num_threads(2)
d = load_digits()
img = torch.tensor(d.images[0] / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)[None, None]     # shape (batch=1, channels=1, 8, 8)
img = F.interpolate(img, size=(24, 24), mode="bilinear")                      # enlarge for visibility
filters = {"vertical edges": [[-1, 0, 1], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, 0, 1]],
           "horizontal edges": [[-1, -2, -1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 1]],
           "blur": [[1 / 9] * 3] * 3}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(10, 2.6))
axes[0].imshow(img[0, 0], cmap="gray"); axes[0].set_title("input (24×24)", fontsize=9)
for ax, (name, k) in zip(axes[1:], filters.items()):
    out = F.conv2d(img, torch.tensor(k, dtype=torch.float32)[None, None], padding=1)
    ax.imshow(out[0, 0], cmap="coolwarm"); ax.set_title(f"{name} → {tuple(out.shape[-2:])}", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes: ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()

A CNN doesn't use hand-made filters — it learns their values by backpropagation, and learns dozens per layer.

The Building Blocks

LayerDoesKey settings
Conv2dLearned filters → feature maps (one per filter)Filters (channels), kernel size (3×3), stride, padding
Activation (ReLU)Non-linearity—
Pooling (max / average)Downsamples, keeps strongest responses; some position tolerance2×2, stride 2 halves width and height
Batch norm, dropoutStability, regularisation (8.7)—
Global average pooling / flatten → denseTurn feature maps into class scoresNumber of classes
Image 1×16×16
→
Conv 16 · ReLU · Pool → 16×8×8
→
Conv 32 · ReLU · Pool → 32×4×4
→
Flatten 512 → Dense
→
10 class logits

Train a CNN

Cell — CNN vs dense network with the same dataPython
import torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X = F.interpolate(torch.tensor(d.images / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None], size=(16, 16), mode="bilinear")
y = torch.tensor(d.target)
tr, te = train_test_split(np.arange(len(y)), test_size=0.3, stratify=d.target, random_state=0)

class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 16, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),     # 16×16 → 8×8
            nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2))    # 8×8 → 4×4
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32 * 4 * 4, n_classes))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.head(self.features(x))

def fit(model, X, y, idx, epochs=12, lr=2e-3, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train(); perm = idx[torch.randperm(len(idx)).numpy()]
        for i in range(0, len(perm), 32):
            b = perm[i:i + 32]; opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(X[b]), y[b]).backward(); opt.step()
    return model

def accuracy(model, X, y, idx):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad(): return (model(X[idx]).argmax(1) == y[idx]).float().mean().item()

torch.manual_seed(0); cnn = fit(SmallCNN(), X, y, tr)
torch.manual_seed(0); dense = fit(nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(),
                                   nn.Linear(128, 10)), X, y, tr)
for name, m in [("CNN", cnn), ("dense", dense)]:
    print(f"{name:<6} parameters {sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()):>6}   test accuracy {accuracy(m, X, y, te):.3f}")

shifted = torch.roll(X, shifts=2, dims=3)                       # move every digit 2 pixels right
print(f"\nimages shifted 2 px right → CNN {accuracy(cnn, shifted, y, te):.3f}, dense {accuracy(dense, shifted, y, te):.3f}")
CNN parameters 9930 test accuracy 0.952 dense parameters 99978 test accuracy 0.948 images shifted 2 px right → CNN 0.587, dense 0.552

The CNN matches the dense network with about a tenth of the parameters, and holds up better when the digit moves — the same filters fire wherever the pattern appears (weight sharing and translation tolerance). On real photos with millions of pixels, that efficiency gap becomes enormous.

What the Network Learned

Cell — first-layer filters and their feature mapsPython
w = cnn.features[0].weight.detach()[:, 0]                  # 16 learned 3×3 filters
maps = cnn.features[:2](X[te[:1]]).detach()[0]              # their responses to one test digit
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(10, 2.8))
for i in range(8):
    axes[0, i].imshow(w[i], cmap="coolwarm"); axes[1, i].imshow(maps[i], cmap="viridis")
    axes[0, i].axis("off"); axes[1, i].axis("off")
axes[0, 0].set_title("filters", fontsize=8, loc="left"); axes[1, 0].set_title("feature maps", fontsize=8, loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()

Landmark Architectures

Model (year)Key idea
LeNet-5 (1998)Conv + pool for digit recognition (cheques)
AlexNet (2012)Deep CNN + ReLU + dropout + GPUs; won ImageNet by a large margin
VGG (2014)Many stacked 3×3 convolutions
ResNet (2015)Residual (skip) connections → 50–150+ layers
EfficientNet, MobileNetAccuracy per compute; mobile-friendly
ConvNeXt; Vision Transformers (ViT)Modernised CNNs; transformer-based image models (Module 11)
Convolutional neural networks slide small learned filters over images, sharing weights across positions so they detect local patterns anywhere with far fewer parameters than dense layers; output size is (n + 2p − k)/s + 1. Typical blocks stack convolution, ReLU and pooling (which downsamples and adds translation tolerance), with batch norm and dropout, followed by global pooling or flattening and dense layers producing class logits. Early layers learn edges, deeper layers shapes and objects. Landmark architectures include LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet with skip connections, efficient mobile networks, and newer ConvNeXt and Vision Transformers.
8.11

Image Classification in Practice

Image classification assigns one label to a whole image: defective or OK, which plant disease, which product. Getting a model that works in the real world needs more than an architecture: consistent preprocessing, data augmentation, a proper validation split, and error analysis with a confusion matrix to see which classes get mixed up and why.

The Pipeline

Collect & label
→
Resize & normalise
→
Augment (train only)
→
Train CNN / fine-tune
→
Evaluate & analyse errors

Data Augmentation

Cell — torchvision transforms create new variants every epochPython
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torchvision.transforms import v2
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
torch.set_num_threads(2)
d = load_digits()
X = F.interpolate(torch.tensor(d.images / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None], size=(16, 16), mode="bilinear")
y = torch.tensor(d.target)
augment = v2.Compose([v2.RandomAffine(degrees=12, translate=(0.12, 0.12), scale=(0.85, 1.1)),
                      v2.RandomErasing(p=0.3, scale=(0.02, 0.08), value=0)])
torch.manual_seed(1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 8, figsize=(10, 1.6))
axes[0].imshow(X[5, 0], cmap="gray"); axes[0].set_title("original", fontsize=8)
for ax in axes[1:]:
    ax.imshow(augment(X[5])[0], cmap="gray")
for ax in axes: ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()

Augmentations should reflect real variation: small rotations and shifts for handwriting, flips for product photos (but not for digits — a flipped 2 isn't a 2), colour jitter for lighting, crops for framing. Never augment validation or test data.

Train With Little Data: Augmentation Helps

Cell — 25 training images per class, tested on shifted, rotated digitsPython
tr_all, te = train_test_split(np.arange(len(y)), test_size=0.4, stratify=d.target, random_state=0)
tr = np.concatenate([tr_all[d.target[tr_all] == c][:25] for c in range(10)])          # 250 images
torch.manual_seed(2)
X_test_shifted = torch.stack([v2.RandomAffine(degrees=10, translate=(0.1, 0.1))(img) for img in X[te]])

def cnn():
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 16, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                         nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(32), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                         nn.Flatten(), nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(512, 10))

def train(use_aug, epochs=40):
    torch.manual_seed(0); m = cnn(); opt = torch.optim.AdamW(m.parameters(), 2e-3, weight_decay=1e-3)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        m.train(); perm = tr[torch.randperm(len(tr)).numpy()]
        for i in range(0, len(perm), 32):
            b = perm[i:i + 32]
            xb = torch.stack([augment(img) for img in X[b]]) if use_aug else X[b]
            opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(m(xb), y[b]).backward(); opt.step()
    return m

def acc(m, Xs, idx_or_y):
    m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad(): return (m(Xs).argmax(1) == idx_or_y).float().mean().item()

for use_aug in (False, True):
    m = train(use_aug)
    print(f"augmentation {'ON ' if use_aug else 'OFF'}  test accuracy {acc(m, X[te], y[te]):.3f}   on shifted/rotated test images {acc(m, X_test_shifted, y[te]):.3f}")
model = m
augmentation OFF test accuracy 0.958 on shifted/rotated test images 0.814 augmentation ON test accuracy 0.960 on shifted/rotated test images 0.943

Error Analysis

Cell — confusion matrix and the most confident mistakesPython
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report
import seaborn as sns
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    probs = F.softmax(model(X[te]), dim=1)
pred = probs.argmax(1)
cm = confusion_matrix(y[te], pred)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 2]})
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt="d", cmap="Blues", cbar=False, ax=axes[0], annot_kws={"fontsize": 7})
axes[0].set_xlabel("predicted"); axes[0].set_ylabel("true")
wrong = np.flatnonzero(pred != y[te])
worst = wrong[np.argsort(-probs[wrong].max(1).values.numpy())][:6]
axes[1].axis("off")
for k, i in enumerate(worst):
    ax = fig.add_axes([0.47 + k * 0.088, 0.25, 0.08, 0.5])
    ax.imshow(X[te[i], 0], cmap="gray"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(f"true {y[te[i]].item()}\npred {pred[i].item()} ({probs[i].max():.0%})", fontsize=7)
axes[1].set_title("most confident mistakes", fontsize=9)
print(classification_report(y[te], pred, digits=3).splitlines()[-1])
weighted avg 0.962 0.960 0.959 719
  • Look at the mistakes: label errors, ambiguous images and systematic confusions (similar-looking classes) each need a different fix
  • Check per-class recall — a 97% average can hide one class at 80%
  • Test on data from the real deployment conditions (different cameras, lighting, phones)
  • Calibrate probabilities if they drive decisions; add an "unsure → human review" band
Image classification pipelines resize and normalise images consistently, apply data augmentation such as random affine transforms, crops, flips and colour jitter only to training data (matching realistic variation), train or fine-tune a CNN with proper validation, and analyse errors with confusion matrices, per-class recall and inspection of the most confident mistakes to separate label noise, ambiguous cases and systematic confusions. Augmentation improves accuracy and robustness when data is scarce, and models must be tested on data from real deployment conditions.
8.12

Transfer Learning

Training a large network from scratch needs millions of labelled images. Transfer learning starts instead from a model already trained on a large dataset and adapts it to your task. Its early layers already detect edges, textures and shapes that are useful almost everywhere, so a few hundred labelled images can be enough. It's the default way to build vision and language models today.

Two Strategies

Feature extraction

Freeze the pretrained layers; train only a new output head. Fast; works with very little data.

Fine-tuning

Then unfreeze some or all layers and train with a small learning rate. Better accuracy with more data or a domain unlike the original.

See It Work

To keep this self-contained, we "pretrain" a CNN on digits 0–4, then transfer it to a new task — digits 5–9 — with only 3 labelled examples per class, and compare against training from scratch.

Cell — pretrain, then transfer with 3 examples per classPython
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F, copy
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
torch.set_num_threads(2)
d = load_digits()
X = F.interpolate(torch.tensor(d.images / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None], size=(16, 16), mode="bilinear")
y = torch.tensor(d.target)
old_task = np.flatnonzero(d.target < 5); new_task = np.flatnonzero(d.target >= 5)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
few = np.concatenate([rng.choice(new_task[d.target[new_task] == c], 3, replace=False) for c in range(5, 10)])
test_new = np.setdiff1d(new_task, few)

def backbone():
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 16, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                         nn.Conv2d(16, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2), nn.Flatten())

def train(model, idx, labels, epochs, lr, params=None, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed); opt = torch.optim.Adam(params or model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train(); perm = idx[torch.randperm(len(idx)).numpy()]
        for i in range(0, len(perm), 32):
            b = perm[i:i + 32]; opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(X[b]), labels[b]).backward(); opt.step()

def acc(model, idx, labels):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad(): return (model(X[idx]).argmax(1) == labels[idx]).float().mean().item()

# 1. pretrain on the big "source" task (digits 0–4)
torch.manual_seed(0); pre = nn.Sequential(backbone(), nn.Linear(512, 5))
train(pre, old_task, y, epochs=15, lr=2e-3)
print(f"pretrained model on its own task (0–4): {acc(pre, old_task, y):.3f}")

y_new = y - 5                                                 # new labels 0..4 for digits 5..9
results = {}
torch.manual_seed(0); scratch = nn.Sequential(backbone(), nn.Linear(512, 5))
train(scratch, few, y_new, epochs=60, lr=2e-3); results["from scratch"] = acc(scratch, test_new, y_new)

frozen = nn.Sequential(copy.deepcopy(pre[0]), nn.Linear(512, 5))     # reuse backbone, new head
for p in frozen[0].parameters(): p.requires_grad = False
train(frozen, few, y_new, epochs=60, lr=5e-3, params=frozen[1].parameters()); results["feature extraction (frozen)"] = acc(frozen, test_new, y_new)

for p in frozen[0].parameters(): p.requires_grad = True              # then unfreeze and fine-tune gently
train(frozen, few, y_new, epochs=20, lr=2e-4); results["+ fine-tuning"] = acc(frozen, test_new, y_new)
for k, v in results.items():
    print(f"{k:<28} accuracy on digits 5–9 with 15 labels: {v:.3f}")
pretrained model on its own task (0–4): 0.999 from scratch accuracy on digits 5–9 with 15 labels: 0.849 feature extraction (frozen) accuracy on digits 5–9 with 15 labels: 0.885 + fine-tuning accuracy on digits 5–9 with 15 labels: 0.881

Reusing the backbone beats training from scratch on 15 labels. Tiny 8×8 digits are easy enough that the gap here is a few points; with real photos and an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet the difference is typically dramatic — often the gap between a usable and a useless model.

With Real Pretrained Models

from torchvision import models
weights = models.ResNet50_Weights.DEFAULT                       # trained on ImageNet (1.3M images, 1,000 classes)
model = models.resnet50(weights=weights)
for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False                                     # 1. freeze the backbone
model.fc = nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, num_classes)         # 2. new head for your classes
preprocess = weights.transforms()                               # 3. use the SAME resizing/normalisation as pretraining
# train the head (lr ≈ 1e-3), then unfreeze layer4 (+ more) and fine-tune with lr ≈ 1e-4 … 1e-5
Your dataSimilar to pretraining dataVery different (X-rays, satellite)
SmallFeature extractionFeature extraction from earlier layers; heavy augmentation
LargeFine-tune top layersFine-tune most or all layers

Model hubs — torchvision, timm, Hugging Face — host thousands of pretrained vision and language models. The same idea underlies fine-tuning BERT for text (Module 9) and LLMs (Module 11).

Transfer learning reuses a model pretrained on a large dataset, whose early layers learn general features, for a new task with limited labels. Feature extraction freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only a new head; fine-tuning then unfreezes some or all layers and trains with a small learning rate to avoid destroying learned features. The new task must use the same preprocessing as pretraining. Strategy depends on data size and similarity to the source domain. It routinely outperforms training from scratch with small datasets and underlies fine-tuning of ResNets, BERT and LLMs from hubs like torchvision, timm and Hugging Face.
8.13

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)

Many kinds of data are sequences: words in a sentence, daily sales, sensor readings, clicks in a session. Order matters, and lengths vary. A recurrent neural network reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state — a running memory — from step to step, using the same weights at every step.
\[ h_t = \tanh\!\big(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t-1} + b\big) \qquad\quad \hat{y}_t = W_y h_t + c \]the same \(W_x, W_h\) are reused at every time step; \(h_t\) summarises everything seen so far
x₁
→
h₁
→
h₂ (+x₂)
→
h₃ (+x₃)
→
output

Sequence Task Shapes

ShapeExample
Many-to-oneReview → sentiment; sensor window → failure in next hour
Many-to-many (aligned)Tagging each word (named entities), frame-by-frame labels
Sequence-to-sequenceTranslation, summarisation (encoder–decoder)
One-to-manyImage → caption

An RNN Step by Hand, Then in PyTorch

Cell — the recurrence, and nn.RNN computing the same thingPython
import torch, torch.nn as nn, numpy as np
torch.set_num_threads(2); torch.manual_seed(0)
rnn = nn.RNN(input_size=1, hidden_size=4, batch_first=True)
seq = torch.tensor([[[0.5], [1.0], [-0.3]]])                    # batch 1, 3 time steps, 1 feature
out, h_last = rnn(seq)

Wx, Wh = rnn.weight_ih_l0, rnn.weight_hh_l0; b = rnn.bias_ih_l0 + rnn.bias_hh_l0
h = torch.zeros(4)
for t in range(3):
    h = torch.tanh(Wx @ seq[0, t] + Wh @ h + b)                    # the formula above
print("manual final state: ", h.detach().numpy().round(4))
print("nn.RNN final state: ", h_last[0, 0].detach().numpy().round(4))
print("output shape (batch, steps, hidden):", tuple(out.shape))
manual final state: [0.083 0.4981 0.2827 0.3731] nn.RNN final state: [0.083 0.4981 0.2827 0.3731] output shape (batch, steps, hidden): (1, 3, 4)

Forecasting a Time Series

Cell — predict tomorrow's demand from the last 28 daysPython
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
t = np.arange(900)
series = 100 + 0.05 * t + 15 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 7) + 8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 30) + rng.normal(0, 3, len(t))
mu, sd = series[:700].mean(), series[:700].std()
s = (series - mu) / sd                                               # scale using training data only
W = 28
Xs = np.stack([s[i:i + W] for i in range(len(s) - W)])[:, :, None]
ys = s[W:]
split = 700 - W
Xtr, ytr = torch.tensor(Xs[:split], dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(ys[:split], dtype=torch.float32)
Xte, yte = torch.tensor(Xs[split:], dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(ys[split:], dtype=torch.float32)

class Forecaster(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cell="rnn", hidden=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.rnn = {"rnn": nn.RNN, "lstm": nn.LSTM, "gru": nn.GRU}[cell](1, hidden, batch_first=True)
        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        seq_out, _ = self.rnn(x)
        return self.out(seq_out[:, -1]).squeeze(-1)                  # many-to-one: use the last step

def fit_forecaster(cell, epochs=30):
    torch.manual_seed(0); m = Forecaster(cell); opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), 3e-3)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(Xtr))
        for i in range(0, len(perm), 64):
            b = perm[i:i + 64]; opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.mse_loss(m(Xtr[b]), ytr[b]).backward()
            nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(m.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step()
    m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad(): pred = m(Xte).numpy() * sd + mu
    return m, pred

rnn_model, pred = fit_forecaster("rnn")
actual = yte.numpy() * sd + mu
naive = series[700 - 7:900 - 7]                                     # same day last week
print(f"test MAE: simple RNN {np.abs(pred - actual).mean():.2f}   seasonal-naive {np.abs(naive - actual).mean():.2f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.8))
ax.plot(range(700, 900), actual, color="#8da0b2", label="actual"); ax.plot(range(700, 900), pred, color="#ffb454", label="RNN forecast")
ax.legend(frameon=False); ax.set_xlabel("day"); plt.tight_layout()
test MAE: simple RNN 3.30 seasonal-naive 7.44

The Weakness: Short Memory

Backpropagation through time multiplies by \(W_h\) and tanh's slope at every step, so gradients from far-back steps vanish (or explode). Plain RNNs struggle to use information more than ~10–20 steps back. The next lesson's gated cells fix that.

Recurrent neural networks process sequences step by step, updating a hidden state h_t = tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_(t−1) + b) with weights shared across time, so they handle variable lengths and support many-to-one, many-to-many, sequence-to-sequence and one-to-many tasks. They are trained with backpropagation through time, often with gradient clipping. Plain RNNs suffer vanishing and exploding gradients, limiting memory to short ranges, which motivated LSTM and GRU cells and, later, attention-based transformers. Forecasts should be compared with seasonal-naive baselines.
8.14

LSTM & GRU

LSTM (long short-term memory) and GRU (gated recurrent unit) add gates — small sigmoid layers that decide what to keep, what to forget and what to output. The LSTM's separate cell state acts like a conveyor belt that carries information across many steps with little change, so gradients survive and long-range patterns can be learned. They were the standard for speech, translation and text before transformers, and remain useful for time series and on-device models.

LSTM Gates

\[ \begin{aligned} f_t &= \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) && \text{forget gate: what to erase from memory} \\ i_t &= \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i),\;\; \tilde{c}_t = \tanh(W_c[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c) && \text{input gate and candidate: what to write} \\ c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t && \text{cell state update (additive!)} \\ o_t &= \sigma(W_o[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o),\;\; h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) && \text{output gate: what to reveal} \end{aligned} \]⊙ = element-wise product · the additive cell update is why gradients don't vanish

GRU: A Simpler Gate Design

\[ z_t = \sigma(W_z[h_{t-1}, x_t]),\;\; r_t = \sigma(W_r[h_{t-1}, x_t]),\;\; \tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W[r_t \odot h_{t-1}, x_t]),\;\; h_t = (1 - z_t) \odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t \]update gate z blends old and new state; reset gate r decides how much past to use · no separate cell state, ~25% fewer parameters

The Memory Test

A task built to need long memory: every step of a 40-step sequence is a random +1 or −1, and the label is simply the first value. To answer, the network must carry one bit across 39 distracting steps.

Cell — plain RNN vs LSTM on remembering the first valuePython
import torch, torch.nn as nn
torch.set_num_threads(2)

def make_data(n, length, seed):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    x = (torch.rand(n, length, 1, generator=g) > 0.5).float() * 2 - 1      # every step is ±1
    return x, (x[:, 0, 0] > 0).long()                                       # label = the first step

class Clf(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cell, hidden=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.rnn = {"RNN": nn.RNN, "LSTM": nn.LSTM}[cell](1, hidden, batch_first=True)
        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden, 2)
        if cell == "LSTM":                                   # common practice: start with the forget gate open
            self.rnn.bias_ih_l0.data[hidden:2 * hidden].fill_(2.0)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.out(self.rnn(x)[0][:, -1])

Xtr, ytr = make_data(4000, 40, 1); Xte, yte = make_data(500, 40, 2)
for cell in ("RNN", "LSTM"):
    torch.manual_seed(0); m = Clf(cell); opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), 3e-3); curve = []
    for step in range(1, 751):
        b = torch.randint(0, 4000, (64,))
        opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.cross_entropy(m(Xtr[b]), ytr[b]).backward()
        nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(m.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step()
        if step % 250 == 0:
            with torch.no_grad(): curve.append(f"{(m(Xte).argmax(1) == yte).float().mean().item():.2f}")
    print(f"{cell:<5} test accuracy after 250 / 500 / 750 steps: {' / '.join(curve)}   (0.50 = guessing)")
for cell, mod in (("RNN", nn.RNN), ("LSTM", nn.LSTM), ("GRU", nn.GRU)):
    print(f"{cell} parameters (hidden 32): {sum(p.numel() for p in mod(1, 32).parameters())}")
RNN test accuracy after 250 / 500 / 750 steps: 0.49 / 0.48 / 0.51 (0.50 = guessing) LSTM test accuracy after 250 / 500 / 750 steps: 0.85 / 0.97 / 1.00 (0.50 = guessing) RNN parameters (hidden 32): 1120 LSTM parameters (hidden 32): 4480 GRU parameters (hidden 32): 3360

The LSTM picks up the signal within a few hundred steps; the plain RNN stays at chance because the gradient from the answer barely reaches step 0. (Given much more training a plain RNN can sometimes get there on a 40-step gap, but it becomes hopeless as gaps grow.) The LSTM has 4 sets of weights (3 gates + candidate), the GRU 3, the plain RNN 1. GRUs usually perform on par with LSTMs; which wins varies by task, so try both.

Practical Options

OptionWhat it doesUse when
Stacked (num_layers=2–3)Layers of RNNs, each reading the previous one's outputsMore complex patterns
BidirectionalOne pass forwards, one backwards, outputs combinedWhole sequence available (text classification, tagging) — not for forecasting
Packed sequences / maskingIgnore padding in variable-length batchesText of different lengths
Dropout between layers, gradient clippingRegularise and stabiliseAlmost always

LSTM / GRU today

Still strong for small/medium time series, streaming and on-device models (cheap per step, constant memory).

Transformers

Replaced RNNs for language: attention looks at all positions at once, trains in parallel, and handles very long contexts (Modules 9, 11).

LSTMs add forget, input and output gates plus a separate cell state updated additively (c_t = f_t ⊙ c_(t−1) + i_t ⊙ candidate), letting information and gradients persist over long sequences and addressing the vanishing-gradient problem of plain RNNs. GRUs merge this into update and reset gates without a separate cell state, using fewer parameters with similar performance. They can be stacked and made bidirectional (when the whole sequence is available), use masking for padding and gradient clipping, and remain useful for time series and streaming, while transformers have replaced them for most language tasks.
8.15

Autoencoders

An autoencoder learns to copy its input to its output through a narrow bottleneck. To succeed, the encoder must compress the input into a small code that keeps what matters, and the decoder must rebuild the input from it. No labels are needed. The result is useful for compression, denoising, anomaly detection and learned features — and the variational version is a generative model.
Input x (64 pixels)
→
Encoder
→
Code z (2–8 numbers)
→
Decoder
→
Reconstruction x̂ · loss = ‖x − x̂‖²

Compress and Rebuild Digits

Cell — a 64 → 8 → 64 autoencoderPython
import torch, torch.nn as nn, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
torch.set_num_threads(2); torch.manual_seed(0)
d = load_digits()
X = torch.tensor(d.data / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32); y = d.target

class AE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, code=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, code))
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(code, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 64), nn.Sigmoid())
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.dec(self.enc(x))

def train_ae(model, inputs, targets, epochs=60):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), 3e-3)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(inputs))
        for i in range(0, len(perm), 64):
            b = perm[i:i + 64]; opt.zero_grad(); nn.functional.mse_loss(model(inputs[b]), targets[b]).backward(); opt.step()
    return model

ae = train_ae(AE(8), X, X)
with torch.no_grad(): recon = ae(X[:8])
print(f"compression 64 → 8 numbers; reconstruction MSE {nn.functional.mse_loss(ae(X), X).item():.4f}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(9, 2.4))
for i in range(8):
    axes[0, i].imshow(X[i].view(8, 8), cmap="gray"); axes[1, i].imshow(recon[i].view(8, 8), cmap="gray")
    axes[0, i].axis("off"); axes[1, i].axis("off")
axes[0, 0].set_title("original", fontsize=8, loc="left"); axes[1, 0].set_title("from 8 numbers", fontsize=8, loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()
compression 64 → 8 numbers; reconstruction MSE 0.0152

Denoising

Cell — train on noisy inputs → clean targetsPython
torch.manual_seed(1)
noisy = (X + 0.35 * torch.randn_like(X)).clamp(0, 1)
dae = train_ae(AE(16), noisy, X)
with torch.no_grad(): cleaned = dae(noisy[:6])
print(f"MSE vs clean: noisy input {nn.functional.mse_loss(noisy, X).item():.4f} → denoised {nn.functional.mse_loss(dae(noisy), X).item():.4f}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 6, figsize=(7, 3.2))
for i in range(6):
    for r, img in enumerate((X[i], noisy[i], cleaned[i])):
        axes[r, i].imshow(img.view(8, 8), cmap="gray"); axes[r, i].axis("off")
for r, t in enumerate(("clean", "noisy", "denoised")): axes[r, 0].set_title(t, fontsize=8, loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()
MSE vs clean: noisy input 0.0676 → denoised 0.0246

Anomaly Detection

Cell — trained only on "normal" items, it reconstructs anomalies badlyPython
torch.manual_seed(2)
normal = X[y != 8]; odd = X[y == 8]                                 # treat 8s as the never-seen anomaly
ae_n = train_ae(AE(4), normal[:1200], normal[:1200])
with torch.no_grad():
    err_normal = ((ae_n(normal[1200:]) - normal[1200:]) ** 2).mean(1).numpy()
    err_odd = ((ae_n(odd) - odd) ** 2).mean(1).numpy()
threshold = np.percentile(err_normal, 95)
print(f"median error: normal {np.median(err_normal):.4f}, anomalies {np.median(err_odd):.4f}")
print(f"threshold at normal 95th percentile flags {np.mean(err_odd > threshold):.0%} of anomalies (and 5% of normal items)")
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
print("ROC-AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(np.r_[np.zeros(len(err_normal)), np.ones(len(err_odd))], np.r_[err_normal, err_odd]), 3))
median error: normal 0.0243, anomalies 0.0481 threshold at normal 95th percentile flags 22% of anomalies (and 5% of normal items) ROC-AUC: 0.874

Anomalies reconstruct about twice as badly on average, but separation is only partial here — an 8 shares strokes with 3s, 5s and 9s the model has learned. Real anomalies (a vibration signature never seen in normal operation) are often more distinct. The same approach monitors machines (sensor patterns), detects fraud and flags defective products when you have plenty of "normal" examples but few labelled failures.

Variants

VariantIdeaUse
Undercomplete (above)Bottleneck smaller than inputCompression, non-linear PCA, features
DenoisingCorrupt input, reconstruct cleanNoise removal, robust features
SparsePenalise active code unitsInterpretable features
ConvolutionalConv encoder, transposed-conv decoderImages
Variational (VAE)Encode to a distribution; sample codes; KL regulariserGeneration; the latent space of image generators like Stable Diffusion
Autoencoders are unsupervised networks with an encoder that compresses input into a low-dimensional code and a decoder that reconstructs it, trained to minimise reconstruction error. They are used for non-linear dimensionality reduction and feature learning, denoising (training noisy inputs against clean targets) and anomaly detection, where a model trained only on normal data reconstructs anomalies poorly so high reconstruction error flags them, with thresholds set from normal-data percentiles. Variants include sparse, convolutional and variational autoencoders; VAEs learn a probabilistic latent space for generation and underpin latent diffusion models.
8.16

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)

A GAN trains two networks against each other. The generator turns random noise into fake samples; the discriminator tries to tell fakes from real data. Each improves by beating the other until the fakes are hard to distinguish from reality. GANs produced the first photorealistic synthetic faces and are used for image enhancement, style transfer and synthetic data — though diffusion models (Module 11) now lead for most image generation.
Random noise z
→
Generator G
→
Fake sample
→
Discriminator D ← real samples
→
"real" or "fake"?
\[ \min_G \max_D \;\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\text{data}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))] \]D maximises its accuracy; G minimises it — in practice G maximises log D(G(z)) for stronger gradients

Train a GAN on Handwritten Digits

Cell — generator and discriminator take turnsPython
import torch, torch.nn as nn, numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
torch.set_num_threads(2); torch.manual_seed(16)
real = torch.tensor(load_digits().data / 16.0 * 2 - 1, dtype=torch.float32)       # scale to [-1, 1]
Z = 16
G = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(Z, 128), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.Tanh())
D = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 128), nn.LeakyReLU(0.2), nn.Dropout(0.3), nn.Linear(128, 1))
