optG = torch.optim.Adam(G.parameters(), 2e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.999))
optD = torch.optim.Adam(D.parameters(), 2e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.999))
bce = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
fixed_z = torch.randn(10, Z)
snapshots = {}
for step in range(1, 6001):
    xb = real[torch.randint(0, len(real), (64,))]
    fake = G(torch.randn(64, Z))
    # 1. discriminator: real → 1 (label-smoothed to 0.9), fake → 0
    optD.zero_grad()
    lossD = bce(D(xb), torch.full((64, 1), 0.9)) + bce(D(fake.detach()), torch.zeros(64, 1))
    lossD.backward(); optD.step()
    # 2. generator: make D call the fakes real
    optG.zero_grad()
    lossG = bce(D(fake), torch.ones(64, 1))
    lossG.backward(); optG.step()
    if step in (200, 1500, 6000):
        with torch.no_grad(): snapshots[step] = G(fixed_z)
        print(f"step {step:>4}  D loss {lossD.item():.3f}  G loss {lossG.item():.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 10, figsize=(9, 3))
for r, (step, imgs) in enumerate(snapshots.items()):
    for c in range(10):
        axes[r, c].imshow(imgs[c].view(8, 8), cmap="gray"); axes[r, c].axis("off")
    axes[r, 0].set_title(f"step {step}", fontsize=8, loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()
step 200 D loss 1.341 G loss 0.752 step 1500 D loss 1.245 G loss 0.926 step 6000 D loss 1.366 G loss 0.881

From noise, the generator learns to produce digit-like shapes it has never been shown directly — it only ever received the discriminator's judgement.

Why GANs Are Hard to Train

ProblemSymptomCommon remedies
Mode collapseGenerator produces only a few kinds of outputMinibatch discrimination, WGAN-GP loss, unrolled training
Non-convergenceLosses oscillate; quality doesn't improveLower learning rates, Adam β₁ = 0.5, spectral normalisation
Discriminator too strongG gets no useful gradientLabel smoothing, dropout/noise in D, fewer D steps
EvaluationLoss doesn't measure qualityFID / Inception score; human inspection

Uses and Responsibility

  • Super-resolution and image restoration, style transfer (CycleGAN), data augmentation for rare classes, synthetic tabular data (CTGAN)
  • DCGAN, StyleGAN (faces), pix2pix (image-to-image) are landmark designs
  • Deepfakes are a serious misuse — provenance, watermarking and detection tools matter, and consent is essential when real people are involved
Generative adversarial networks train a generator that maps random noise to samples and a discriminator that classifies samples as real or fake in a minimax game; training alternates discriminator updates on real and detached fake batches with generator updates that try to make fakes be classified as real. GANs are hard to train because of mode collapse, oscillation and an overpowering discriminator, mitigated by label smoothing, Adam with β₁ = 0.5, spectral normalisation and Wasserstein losses, and they are evaluated with FID rather than loss. Uses include super-resolution, style transfer and synthetic data; diffusion models now lead image generation, and deepfake misuse calls for provenance and consent.
8.17

Object Detection

Classification says what is in an image. Object detection says what and where: it outputs a bounding box, a class and a confidence for every object — cars and pedestrians for driver assistance, products on a shelf, defects on a circuit board, helmets on a construction site. This lesson covers how detections are represented and scored (IoU, NMS, mAP) and how the main detector families work.

Vision Tasks Compared

TaskOutputExample models
ClassificationOne label per imageResNet, EfficientNet, ViT
LocalisationLabel + one boxCNN with a box-regression head (project 8.20)
DetectionMany boxes + labels + scoresYOLO, SSD, Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, DETR
Semantic segmentationClass for every pixelU-Net, DeepLab
Instance segmentationPixel mask per objectMask R-CNN, SAM (segment anything)

Intersection over Union (IoU)

\[ \text{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{\text{area}(A \cap B)}{\text{area}(A \cup B)} \]boxes as (x₁, y₁, x₂, y₂) · a prediction usually counts as correct when IoU ≥ 0.5 with a true box of the same class
Cell — IoU from scratch, checked against torchvisionPython
import torch, numpy as np
from torchvision.ops import box_iou, nms

def iou(a, b):
    x1, y1 = max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1]); x2, y2 = min(a[2], b[2]), min(a[3], b[3])
    inter = max(0, x2 - x1) * max(0, y2 - y1)
    area = lambda r: (r[2] - r[0]) * (r[3] - r[1])
    return inter / (area(a) + area(b) - inter)

truth = [50, 50, 150, 150]
for pred in ([55, 60, 150, 155], [100, 100, 200, 200], [200, 200, 250, 250]):
    print(f"pred {pred}: IoU {iou(truth, pred):.3f}   torchvision {box_iou(torch.tensor([truth], dtype=torch.float), torch.tensor([pred], dtype=torch.float)).item():.3f}")
pred [55, 60, 150, 155]: IoU 0.816 torchvision 0.816 pred [100, 100, 200, 200]: IoU 0.143 torchvision 0.143 pred [200, 200, 250, 250]: IoU 0.000 torchvision 0.000

Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)

Detectors propose many overlapping boxes for the same object. NMS keeps the highest-scoring box and removes others that overlap it by more than a threshold.

Cell — NMS by hand vs torchvision.ops.nmsPython
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, matplotlib.patches as patches
boxes = torch.tensor([[48, 52, 152, 148], [55, 45, 158, 155], [45, 60, 140, 150],      # three guesses for object 1
                      [210, 80, 300, 190], [205, 85, 295, 180],                         # two for object 2
                      [120, 120, 230, 200]], dtype=torch.float)                         # a weak, overlapping guess
scores = torch.tensor([0.92, 0.85, 0.60, 0.88, 0.70, 0.40])

def my_nms(boxes, scores, thr=0.5):
    order, keep = scores.argsort(descending=True).tolist(), []
    while order:
        best = order.pop(0); keep.append(best)
        order = [i for i in order if iou(boxes[best].tolist(), boxes[i].tolist()) < thr]
    return keep

print("kept (mine):       ", my_nms(boxes, scores))
print("kept (torchvision):", nms(boxes, scores, 0.5).tolist())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3))
for ax, idx, title in [(axes[0], range(6), "raw detections"), (axes[1], nms(boxes, scores, 0.5).tolist(), "after NMS")]:
    ax.set_xlim(0, 320); ax.set_ylim(220, 0); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for i in idx:
        x1, y1, x2, y2 = boxes[i].tolist()
        ax.add_patch(patches.Rectangle((x1, y1), x2 - x1, y2 - y1, fill=False, color="#ffb454", lw=1.5))
        ax.text(x1, y1 - 3, f"{scores[i]:.2f}", color="#ffb454", fontsize=7)
plt.tight_layout()
kept (mine): [0, 3, 5] kept (torchvision): [0, 3, 5]

How Detectors Work

FamilyIdeaTrade-off
Two-stage (Faster R-CNN)A region proposal network suggests likely object regions; a second head classifies and refines eachAccurate, slower
One-stage (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet)Predict boxes and classes for a grid of locations (and anchor shapes) in a single passReal-time; YOLO variants dominate practical use
Transformer (DETR, RT-DETR)Predict a set of objects directly with attention; no anchors or NMSElegant; strong with enough data
Open-vocabulary (OWL-ViT, Grounding DINO)Detect objects described in text, zero-shotNo training for new classes; less precise

All share a CNN or transformer backbone (usually pretrained — transfer learning), a neck that combines features at several scales (small and large objects), and heads that predict class scores and box offsets.

Using a Pretrained Detector

# torchvision (Faster R-CNN, pretrained on COCO's 80 everyday classes)
from torchvision.models.detection import fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2, FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_V2_Weights
weights = FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_V2_Weights.DEFAULT
model = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2(weights=weights).eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model([weights.transforms()(image)])[0]        # dict: boxes, labels, scores
keep = out["scores"] > 0.7

# Ultralytics YOLO: train on your own labelled boxes in a few lines
from ultralytics import YOLO
model = YOLO("yolo11n.pt")                                # small pretrained model
model.train(data="shelf.yaml", epochs=50, imgsz=640)      # images + one .txt label file per image
results = model("store_aisle.jpg")

Evaluating: mAP

  • For each class: sort detections by confidence; a detection is a true positive if IoU ≥ threshold with an unmatched true box
  • Compute the precision–recall curve; AP = area under it
  • mAP@0.5 = mean AP over classes at IoU 0.5; mAP@0.5:0.95 (COCO) averages over stricter IoU thresholds too
  • Also check speed (frames per second) and performance on small objects
Labelling boxes is the expensive part. Tools like CVAT, Label Studio and Roboflow help; start from a pretrained detector, label a few hundred images per class, and add more where the model fails.
Object detection predicts bounding boxes, classes and confidence scores for every object. Box overlap is measured by Intersection over Union, used to match predictions to ground truth (typically IoU ≥ 0.5) and in non-maximum suppression, which keeps the highest-scoring box and discards overlapping duplicates. Two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN propose regions then classify them (accurate), one-stage detectors like YOLO and SSD predict over a grid in one pass (real-time), and transformer detectors like DETR predict object sets without NMS; all use pretrained backbones and multi-scale necks. Performance is measured with mAP over classes and IoU thresholds, plus speed.
8.18

Face Recognition

Face recognition can't be an ordinary classifier: a company adds new employees every week, and you can't retrain a model for each one. Instead, a network learns to map any face to an embedding — a vector where photos of the same person land close together and different people land far apart. Recognising someone becomes comparing vectors. The same embedding idea powers product search, duplicate detection and semantic search over text.

The Pipeline

Detect face
→
Align (eyes, nose)
→
Embed → 128–512 numbers
→
Compare (cosine similarity)
→
Same person? / Who is it?
TaskQuestionHow
Verification (1:1)Is this the person they claim to be? (phone unlock, KYC)similarity(selfie, ID photo) > threshold
Identification (1:N)Who is this, among enrolled people?Nearest enrolled embedding (vector search), if above threshold
ClusteringGroup photos by personCluster the embeddings

Learning Embeddings for Unseen Identities

Faces need consent and careful handling, so this demo uses handwriting as a stand-in: each digit plays the role of a "person". The network is trained on digits 0–6 only, then asked to verify pairs of never-seen identities 7, 8 and 9 — exactly the open-set situation of a new employee.

Cell — train an embedding network with a normalised (cosine) classifierPython
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, roc_curve
torch.set_num_threads(2); torch.manual_seed(18)
d = load_digits()
X = F.interpolate(torch.tensor(d.images / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None], size=(16, 16), mode="bilinear")
y = torch.tensor(d.target)
seen, unseen = np.flatnonzero(d.target <= 6), np.flatnonzero(d.target >= 7)

embed = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(32), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                      nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                      nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 16, 64))                  # → 64-dimensional embedding
centres = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(7, 64))                                    # one learned direction per training identity
opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(embed.parameters()) + [centres], 2e-3)
for epoch in range(15):
    embed.train(); perm = seen[torch.randperm(len(seen)).numpy()]
    for i in range(0, len(perm), 64):
        b = perm[i:i + 64]
        e = F.normalize(embed(X[b]), dim=1)
        logits = 16 * e @ F.normalize(centres, dim=1).T - 0.35 * 16 * F.one_hot(y[b], 7)   # cosine logits with a margin (CosFace-style)
        opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(logits, y[b]).backward(); opt.step()

embed.eval()
with torch.no_grad(): E = F.normalize(embed(X[unseen]), dim=1)
labels = y[unseen].numpy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
i, j = rng.integers(0, len(unseen), 4000), rng.integers(0, len(unseen), 4000)
mask = i != j
sim = (E[i[mask]] * E[j[mask]]).sum(1).numpy(); same = (labels[i[mask]] == labels[j[mask]]).astype(int)
print(f"verification on identities never seen in training: ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(same, sim):.3f}")
print(f"mean cosine similarity — same identity {sim[same == 1].mean():.2f}, different {sim[same == 0].mean():.2f}")
fpr, tpr, thr = roc_curve(same, sim)
k = np.searchsorted(fpr, 0.01)
print(f"at a 1% false-accept rate: threshold {thr[k]:.2f}, true-accept rate {tpr[k]:.1%}")
verification on identities never seen in training: ROC-AUC 0.828 mean cosine similarity — same identity 0.49, different 0.05 at a 1% false-accept rate: threshold 0.74, true-accept rate 27.4%

Even trained on only seven "identities", the embedding separates new ones far better than chance. Production face models are trained on millions of images of hundreds of thousands of people and reach well over 99% true-accept rates at very low false-accept rates — the method is the same.

Identification by Nearest Neighbour

Cell — enrol one example per new identity, then identify the restPython
gallery_idx = [np.flatnonzero(labels == c)[0] for c in (7, 8, 9)]           # one "enrolment photo" each
gallery = E[gallery_idx]; probes = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(labels)), gallery_idx)
sims = E[probes] @ gallery.T
pred = np.array([7, 8, 9])[sims.argmax(1).numpy()]
print(f"1-shot identification accuracy for 3 new identities: {(pred == labels[probes]).mean():.3f}  (chance 0.333)")
1-shot identification accuracy for 3 new identities: 0.766 (chance 0.333)

Losses That Shape Embeddings

LossIdea
Contrastive (Siamese)Pull same-person pairs together, push different pairs beyond a margin
Triplet (FaceNet)anchor–positive distance + margin < anchor–negative distance
Angular margin (CosFace, ArcFace)Classification on normalised embeddings with a margin — used by most modern systems (as above)

Responsible Use

  • Face data is biometric personal data: get explicit consent, minimise storage, and follow law (India's DPDP Act 2023, GDPR) — some uses are restricted or banned
  • Measure error rates across demographic groups; accuracy gaps have caused wrongful outcomes
  • Choose thresholds by the cost of a false accept vs a false reject; add liveness detection against photos and masks
  • Keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions
Face recognition detects and aligns faces, maps each to an embedding vector with a deep network, and compares embeddings with cosine similarity: verification (1:1) thresholds the similarity of two faces, identification (1:N) finds the nearest enrolled embedding, and clustering groups photos. Embeddings generalise to identities never seen in training, so new people are enrolled without retraining. They are learned with contrastive, triplet or angular-margin losses such as ArcFace and CosFace, and thresholds are set from false-accept and false-reject trade-offs. Biometric use requires consent, legal compliance, fairness testing across groups, liveness checks and human oversight.
8.19

Deploying Deep Learning Models

Deep models bring deployment questions that classical models don't: they're big, they're slow on CPUs, inputs (images, audio) need identical preprocessing, and they may need to run on a phone or a camera. This lesson covers saving and exporting models, making them smaller and faster (quantisation), serving them behind an API, and the options for edge devices.

Save Weights, Export Graphs

Cell — state_dict, torch.export and an equivalence checkPython
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F, numpy as np, os, time
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
torch.set_num_threads(2); torch.manual_seed(19)
d = load_digits()
X = F.interpolate(torch.tensor(d.images / 16.0, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None], size=(16, 16), mode="bilinear")
y = torch.tensor(d.target)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                      nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                      nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(1024, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), 1e-3)
for epoch in range(15):
    for i in range(0, 1400, 64):
        opt.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(model(X[i:i + 64]), y[i:i + 64]).backward(); opt.step()
model.eval()

torch.save(model.state_dict(), "digits_cnn.pt")                 # 1. weights only — needs the model code to reload
exported = torch.export.export(model, (X[:4],),                  # 2. self-contained graph (torch.export)
                               dynamic_shapes=({0: torch.export.Dim("batch")},))   # any batch size
torch.export.save(exported, "digits_cnn.pt2")
reloaded = torch.export.load("digits_cnn.pt2").module()          # runs without the original Python class
with torch.no_grad():
    same = torch.allclose(model(X[1400:]), reloaded(X[1400:]), atol=1e-5)
    acc = (reloaded(X[1400:]).argmax(1) == y[1400:]).float().mean().item()
print(f"state_dict {os.path.getsize('digits_cnn.pt') / 1024:.0f} KB | exported program {os.path.getsize('digits_cnn.pt2') / 1024:.0f} KB | outputs identical: {same} | held-out accuracy {acc:.3f}")
state_dict 1112 KB | exported program 2929 KB | outputs identical: True | held-out accuracy 0.924
# ONNX: a framework-neutral format, run by ONNX Runtime on CPU, GPU, mobile, browsers
torch.onnx.export(model, X[:1], "digits_cnn.onnx", input_names=["image"], output_names=["logits"],
                  dynamic_axes={"image": {0: "batch"}})
import onnxruntime as ort
session = ort.InferenceSession("digits_cnn.onnx")
logits = session.run(None, {"image": X[:4].numpy()})[0]

Smaller and Faster: Quantisation

Cell — dynamic int8 quantisation of the dense layersPython
import io, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
q = torch.ao.quantization.quantize_dynamic(model, {nn.Linear}, dtype=torch.qint8)
def size_kb(m):
    buf = io.BytesIO(); torch.save(m.state_dict(), buf); return buf.tell() / 1024
def latency(m, reps=200):
    xb = X[:1]
    with torch.no_grad():
        m(xb); t = time.perf_counter()
        for _ in range(reps): m(xb)
    return (time.perf_counter() - t) / reps * 1000
with torch.no_grad():
    acc_q = (q(X[1400:]).argmax(1) == y[1400:]).float().mean().item()
print(f"float32: {size_kb(model):6.0f} KB  {latency(model):.2f} ms/image  accuracy {acc:.3f}")
print(f"int8   : {size_kb(q):6.0f} KB  {latency(q):.2f} ms/image  accuracy {acc_q:.3f}")
float32: 1112 KB 0.12 ms/image accuracy 0.924 int8 : 337 KB 0.14 ms/image accuracy 0.927

The int8 model is about a third of the size with the same accuracy. Speed gains depend on hardware and model size: on this tiny network the conversion overhead cancels them, while large models on CPUs or mobile NPUs typically run 2–4× faster.

TechniqueEffect
Quantisation (float32 → int8 / 4-bit)~4× smaller, faster on CPUs and NPUs, small accuracy loss (check it)
PruningRemove unimportant weights or channels
Knowledge distillationTrain a small "student" to mimic a big "teacher"
Efficient architecturesMobileNet, EfficientNet-Lite, YOLO-nano for edge devices
Compilers / runtimesONNX Runtime, TensorRT (NVIDIA), OpenVINO (Intel), Core ML, TFLite / LiteRT

Serving Behind an API

# app.py — FastAPI image endpoint;  run: uvicorn app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
from fastapi import FastAPI, UploadFile
from PIL import Image
import io, torch, torchvision.transforms.v2 as T

app = FastAPI()
model = torch.export.load("digits_cnn.pt2").module()             # load once at start-up
prep = T.Compose([T.Grayscale(), T.Resize((16, 16)), T.ToImage(), T.ToDtype(torch.float32, scale=True)])

@app.post("/predict")
async def predict(file: UploadFile):
    img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(await file.read()))
    with torch.inference_mode():
        probs = model(prep(img)[None]).softmax(1)[0]
    top = int(probs.argmax())
    return {"label": top, "confidence": round(float(probs[top]), 4)}
  • Preprocessing at serving time must match training exactly (same resize, normalisation, channel order)
  • Batch requests on GPU servers (TorchServe, NVIDIA Triton, Ray Serve) for throughput
  • Containerise with pinned versions; scale on Kubernetes or managed endpoints (Azure ML, SageMaker, Vertex AI) — Module 10
  • Monitor latency, errors, input drift (image brightness, resolution, new camera types) and accuracy on sampled, human-labelled traffic

Deep-learning models are saved as weights (PyTorch state_dict) or exported as self-contained graphs (torch.export programs, ONNX; TorchScript in older code) that load without the training code and run in optimised runtimes such as ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO, Core ML or TFLite. Quantisation to int8, pruning, distillation and efficient architectures shrink and speed up models for CPUs and edge devices, with accuracy re-checked afterwards. Models are served via APIs (FastAPI, TorchServe, Triton) with identical preprocessing, request batching on GPUs, containers and autoscaling, or in batch, mobile, edge and browser targets, and monitored for latency, input drift and accuracy.

Deep Learning Project: Shelf Product Locator

The brief: a grocery chain wants shelf cameras to spot which product type is in view and exactly where it sits, to check planogram compliance. You'll build the core model: a CNN with two heads — one classifies the product (can, box or pouch), the other regresses its bounding box. Real projects start from labelled store photos and a pretrained detector (8.17); here the images are generated so the whole pipeline runs in under a minute, but every step — data, model, multi-task loss, IoU evaluation, error review, export — is the real one.
1 · Data + labels
→
2 · Two-head CNN
→
3 · Train: CE + box loss
→
4 · Evaluate: accuracy, IoU
→
5 · Review & export

1 · Generate labelled shelf images

Cell — 48×48 images: noisy shelf background, one product, its class and boxPython
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.set_num_threads(2)
S, CLASSES = 48, ["can", "box", "pouch"]
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:S, 0:S]

def make_image(rng):
    img = rng.normal(0.3, 0.12, (S, S)) + 0.1 * (yy % 16 < 2)             # noisy texture + shelf edges
    for _ in range(rng.integers(3, 7)):                                    # clutter: bright blobs
        cy, cx = rng.integers(0, S, 2); img += 0.4 * np.exp(-((yy - cy) ** 2 + (xx - cx) ** 2) / rng.uniform(2, 10))
    cls = rng.integers(3)
    w, h = rng.integers(8, 22), rng.integers(8, 22)
    x0, y0 = rng.integers(0, S - w), rng.integers(0, S - h)
    cx, cy = x0 + w / 2, y0 + h / 2
    if cls == 0:                                                           # can: filled ellipse
        mask = ((xx - cx) / (w / 2)) ** 2 + ((yy - cy) / (h / 2)) ** 2 <= 1
    elif cls == 1:                                                         # box: rectangle with a stripe
        mask = (xx >= x0) & (xx < x0 + w) & (yy >= y0) & (yy < y0 + h)
    else:                                                                  # pouch: triangle (wide base)
        mask = (yy >= y0) & (yy < y0 + h) & (np.abs(xx - cx) <= (yy - y0 + 1) / h * w / 2)
    img[mask] = rng.uniform(0.5, 0.9) + rng.normal(0, 0.05, mask.sum())
    if cls == 1: img[mask & (np.abs(yy - cy) < 2)] = 0.35
    if rng.random() < 0.4:                                                 # a price tag partly covers the product
        tx = rng.integers(x0, x0 + w); img[:, max(tx - 2, 0):tx + 2][(yy[:, :1] > cy).ravel()] = 0.15
    ys_, xs_ = np.nonzero(mask)
    box = np.array([xs_.min(), ys_.min(), xs_.max() + 1, ys_.max() + 1], dtype=np.float32)   # tight box (x1, y1, x2, y2)
    return np.clip(img, 0, 1).astype(np.float32), cls, box

rng = np.random.default_rng(820)
data = [make_image(rng) for _ in range(5000)]
X = torch.tensor(np.stack([d[0] for d in data]))[:, None]
y = torch.tensor([d[1] for d in data])
B = torch.tensor(np.stack([d[2] for d in data])) / S                       # boxes normalised to 0–1
tr, va, te = np.arange(0, 3500), np.arange(3500, 4200), np.arange(4200, 5000)
print(f"images {tuple(X.shape)}, class counts {np.bincount(y.numpy()).tolist()}, splits {len(tr)}/{len(va)}/{len(te)}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 6, figsize=(10, 2))
for ax, i in zip(axes, range(6)):
    ax.imshow(X[i, 0], cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    x1, y1, x2, y2 = (B[i] * S).tolist()
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x1 - 0.5, y1 - 0.5), x2 - x1, y2 - y1, fill=False, color="#6de5a0", lw=1.5))
    ax.set_title(CLASSES[y[i]], fontsize=8); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
images (5000, 1, 48, 48), class counts [1667, 1677, 1656], splits 3500/700/800

2 · A CNN with two heads

Cell — shared backbone, class head and box headPython
class Locator(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        def block(i, o): return nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(i, o, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(o), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2))
        self.backbone = nn.Sequential(block(1, 16), block(16, 32), block(32, 64), nn.Flatten())   # 48 → 24 → 12 → 6
        self.cls_head = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64 * 36, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.2), nn.Linear(128, 3))
        self.box_head = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64 * 36, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 4), nn.Sigmoid())
    def forward(self, x):
        f = self.backbone(x)
        return self.cls_head(f), self.box_head(f)

model = Locator()
print(f"parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()):,}")
parameters: 614,503

3 · Train with a combined loss

\[ \mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\text{CrossEntropy}(\text{class})}_{\text{what}} + \lambda \cdot \underbrace{\text{SmoothL1}(\text{box})}_{\text{where}} \]λ balances the two tasks; Smooth L1 (Huber) is less sensitive to occasional large box errors than squared error
Cell — training loop with validation-based checkpointingPython
from torchvision.ops import box_iou
import copy, time
torch.manual_seed(0)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), 2e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=3e-3, total_steps=12 * (len(tr) // 64 + 1))
LAMBDA = 5.0

def evaluate(idx):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits, box = model(X[idx])
    acc = (logits.argmax(1) == y[idx]).float().mean().item()
    ious = box_iou(box * S, B[idx] * S).diagonal()
    return acc, ious.mean().item(), (ious >= 0.5).float().mean().item()

best, t0 = -1, time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, 13):
    model.train(); perm = tr[torch.randperm(len(tr)).numpy()]
    for i in range(0, len(perm), 64):
        b = perm[i:i + 64]
        logits, box = model(X[b])
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y[b]) + LAMBDA * F.smooth_l1_loss(box, B[b], beta=0.02)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); sched.step()
    acc, miou, hit = evaluate(va)
    if acc + miou > best:
        best, best_state = acc + miou, copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
    if epoch % 3 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:>2}  loss {loss.item():.3f}  val accuracy {acc:.3f}  val mean IoU {miou:.3f}  IoU≥0.5 {hit:.1%}")
model.load_state_dict(best_state)
print(f"trained in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f}s on CPU")
epoch 3 loss 0.854 val accuracy 0.857 val mean IoU 0.563 IoU≥0.5 70.0% epoch 6 loss 0.212 val accuracy 0.459 val mean IoU 0.589 IoU≥0.5 72.0% epoch 9 loss 0.066 val accuracy 0.974 val mean IoU 0.723 IoU≥0.5 93.1% epoch 12 loss 0.050 val accuracy 0.989 val mean IoU 0.744 IoU≥0.5 94.4% trained in 25s on CPU

4 · Evaluate once on the test set

Cell — classification, localisation and a combined "correct detection" ratePython
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    logits, box = model(X[te])
pred = logits.argmax(1); ious = box_iou(box * S, B[te] * S).diagonal()
correct = (pred == y[te]) & (ious >= 0.5)
print(classification_report(y[te], pred, target_names=CLASSES, digits=3))
print(f"mean IoU {ious.mean():.3f} · IoU ≥ 0.5: {(ious >= 0.5).float().mean():.1%} · IoU ≥ 0.75: {(ious >= 0.75).float().mean():.1%}")
print(f"correct detection (right class AND IoU ≥ 0.5): {correct.float().mean():.1%}")
centre_err = ((box[:, :2] + box[:, 2:]) / 2 - (B[te, :2] + B[te, 2:]) / 2).abs().mul(S).mean().item()
print(f"average centre error: {centre_err:.2f} pixels on a {S}×{S} image")

5 · Review predictions and failures

Cell — green = true box, orange = predicted; worst cases on the bottom rowPython
worst = torch.argsort(ious)[:6].tolist()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 6, figsize=(10, 3.8))
for row, picks in enumerate([list(range(6)), worst]):
    for ax, k in zip(axes[row], picks):
        i = te[k]; ax.imshow(X[i, 0], cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1); ax.axis("off")
        for bx, c in [(B[i] * S, "#6de5a0"), (box[k] * S, "#ffb454")]:
            x1, y1, x2, y2 = bx.tolist()
            ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x1 - 0.5, y1 - 0.5), x2 - x1, y2 - y1, fill=False, color=c, lw=1.4))
        ax.set_title(f"{CLASSES[pred[k]]} · IoU {ious[k]:.2f}", fontsize=7, color="#ff7c7c" if not correct[k] else "#e8eef5")
axes[0, 0].text(-8, 24, "typical", rotation=90, fontsize=8, va="center"); axes[1, 0].text(-8, 24, "worst", rotation=90, fontsize=8, va="center")
plt.tight_layout()

Error review drives the next iteration: are failures small products, products near the image edge, or clutter that looks like a product? Each suggests a fix — more examples of that case, augmentation, higher resolution, or a detector that handles several objects.

6 · Export for the store edge device

Cell — export, reload and verify; measure per-image latencyPython
import os
exported = torch.export.export(model.eval(), (X[te[:4]],), dynamic_shapes=({0: torch.export.Dim("batch")},))
torch.export.save(exported, "shelf_locator.pt2")
runtime = torch.export.load("shelf_locator.pt2").module()
with torch.no_grad():
    l2, b2 = runtime(X[te])
    t = time.perf_counter()
    for i in range(100): runtime(X[te[i:i + 1]])
print(f"exported {os.path.getsize('shelf_locator.pt2') / 1e6:.1f} MB · identical outputs: {torch.allclose(b2, box, atol=1e-5)} · "

From Prototype to Production

StepWhat changes for real store images
DataPhotograph real shelves under varied lighting and angles; label boxes in CVAT/Label Studio; hundreds of images per product type
ModelFine-tune a pretrained detector (YOLO, Faster R-CNN) — many products per image, many classes
EvaluationmAP@0.5:0.95 per class; per-store and per-lighting breakdowns
DeploymentQuantised model on an edge box (Jetson/OpenVINO) beside the camera; send only results, not video
MonitoringSample frames for human review; retrain as packaging and planograms change
The shelf-locator project builds a single-object localisation model end to end: generating labelled images with class and bounding box, a CNN backbone with separate classification and box-regression heads (sigmoid-normalised coordinates), a multi-task loss combining cross-entropy and Smooth L1 weighted by λ, training with AdamW, a one-cycle schedule and validation checkpointing, test evaluation with per-class metrics, mean IoU and the share of predictions that are both correctly classified and overlap at IoU ≥ 0.5, review of worst cases, and export with torch.export for edge deployment. Production versions fine-tune pretrained multi-object detectors on labelled real images and are evaluated with mAP.
8.21

Interview Questions

Common deep-learning interview questions with concise, spoken-style answers and the lesson to revisit. Try answering each out loud first.

Foundations

QuestionStrong answer
Why do neural networks need non-linear activations?Without them, any number of layers collapses into one linear transformation, so the network can only learn linear boundaries. (8.2)
Why is ReLU preferred over sigmoid in hidden layers?Its gradient is 1 for positive inputs, so it doesn't saturate and cause vanishing gradients; it's also cheap. Downsides: dead units (use Leaky ReLU/GELU). (8.2)
Explain backpropagation.The chain rule applied backwards from the loss through each layer, reusing forward-pass values, giving the gradient for every weight in one pass; an optimizer then updates the weights. (8.4)
What causes vanishing / exploding gradients, and how do you fix them?Products of many small or large derivatives through depth or time. Fixes: ReLU, He/Xavier init, batch/layer norm, residual connections, LSTM/GRU, gradient clipping. (8.4, 8.7)
Which loss for which task?MSE/Huber for regression; binary cross-entropy (sigmoid) for binary and multi-label; categorical cross-entropy (softmax) for multi-class — fed raw logits for stability. (8.3)
SGD vs Adam?Adam adapts per-parameter step sizes with momentum — fast, robust default (AdamW with weight decay). Well-tuned SGD with momentum and a schedule can generalise slightly better on vision. (8.5)
What does batch size affect?Gradient noise, speed and memory. Larger batches use hardware better but may need a higher learning rate and can generalise slightly worse; use gradient accumulation when memory-bound. (8.5, 8.9)

Training

QuestionStrong answer
How does dropout work, and what happens at inference?Randomly zeroes units during training so the network can't depend on any single one (an implicit ensemble). At inference it's off; activations are scaled during training so expectations match. (8.7)
What does batch normalisation do?Normalises each layer's inputs per mini-batch, then rescales with learned parameters — stabilises and speeds training, allows higher learning rates. Uses running statistics at inference (hence model.eval()). (8.7)
Your loss is NaN. What do you check?Learning rate too high, bad inputs (NaN/inf, unscaled), log of zero in a custom loss, exploding gradients (clip), mixed-precision overflow. First overfit one batch at a lower rate. (8.7)
How do you tune a deep network efficiently?Learning rate first (range test), then batch size and capacity, then regularisation; random/Bayesian search with early pruning; screen on small budgets; confirm across seeds. (8.8)
How would you train a model that doesn't fit in GPU memory?Mixed precision, smaller batch with gradient accumulation, gradient checkpointing, then sharding (FSDP/DeepSpeed) across GPUs. (8.9)

Architectures and Applications

QuestionStrong answer
Why do CNNs work well for images?Local filters with shared weights detect patterns anywhere (translation tolerance) with far fewer parameters; stacking builds a hierarchy from edges to objects; pooling adds robustness. (8.10)
What problem do residual connections solve?Very deep plain networks are hard to optimise; skip connections let gradients flow directly and let layers learn small corrections, enabling 100+ layers. (8.7, 8.10)
When and how do you use transfer learning?Almost always with limited data: freeze a pretrained backbone and train a new head, then fine-tune upper layers with a small learning rate, using the original preprocessing. (8.12)
LSTM vs GRU vs transformer?LSTM: gates + cell state for long memory. GRU: simpler, fewer parameters, similar results. Transformers use attention over all positions, train in parallel and dominate language; RNNs remain useful for streaming and small time-series models. (8.13–8.14)
What is an autoencoder used for?Unsupervised compression and features, denoising, and anomaly detection via reconstruction error; VAEs are generative. (8.15)
Explain how a GAN trains and why it's difficult.Generator vs discriminator in a minimax game; unstable because each changes the other's objective — mode collapse, oscillation. Mitigations: label smoothing, spectral norm, WGAN-GP; evaluate with FID. (8.16)
What are IoU, NMS and mAP?IoU measures box overlap; NMS removes duplicate boxes overlapping a higher-scoring one; mAP averages precision–recall area over classes (and IoU thresholds). (8.17)
How does face recognition handle new people without retraining?It learns an embedding space (triplet/ArcFace losses); new people are enrolled by storing their embeddings, and matching uses cosine similarity with a threshold. (8.18)
How would you make a model fast enough for a phone?Efficient architecture (MobileNet), quantisation (int8), pruning or distillation, export to Core ML/TFLite/ONNX, and measure latency on the device. (8.19)

Quick-Fire Coding Check

Cell — "write a PyTorch training step" and "count the parameters of a conv layer"Python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
def train_step(model, batch, opt, loss_fn):
    x, y = batch
    model.train()
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    return loss.item()

torch.manual_seed(0)
m = nn.Linear(3, 2); opt = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), 0.1)
print("loss:", round(train_step(m, (torch.randn(8, 3), torch.randint(0, 2, (8,))), opt, nn.CrossEntropyLoss()), 4))

conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3)
print("Conv2d(3→16, 3×3) parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in conv.parameters()), "= 16 × (3 × 3 × 3) + 16 biases =", 16 * 27 + 16)
loss: 0.4948 Conv2d(3→16, 3×3) parameters: 448 = 16 × (3 × 3 × 3) + 16 biases = 448
Deep-learning interviews cover why non-linear activations and ReLU matter, backpropagation and vanishing or exploding gradients, loss and optimizer choices, batch size, dropout and batch normalisation behaviour at training versus inference, debugging NaN losses, efficient tuning, memory-saving techniques, why CNNs and residual connections work, transfer learning, LSTM/GRU versus transformers, autoencoders, GAN training difficulties, detection metrics (IoU, NMS, mAP), embedding-based face recognition and making models fast for mobile — answered directly, then with reasoning and an example.

→
Architecture (MLP · CNN · RNN)

Deep learning builds networks of neurons with non-linear activations, computes predictions by forward propagation and losses such as cross-entropy, learns by backpropagation with optimizers like AdamW and learning-rate schedules, and trains reliably with initialisation, normalisation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping, residual connections, tuning and GPUs. CNNs handle images and power classification, transfer learning, detection and embedding-based recognition; RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs handle sequences; autoencoders and GANs learn representations and generate data; and models are exported, quantised and served on cloud, mobile and edge devices.
